title: Meditations
text:
1. From my grandfather Verus: nobility of character, and a temper free from anger.
2. From the reputation my father left behind, and my memory of him: modesty and a manly bearing.
3. From my mother: piety and generosity; to abstain not only from doing wrong but even from dwelling on such thoughts; and further, a simple way of life, far removed from the habits of the rich.
4. From my great-grandfather: not to have attended the public schools, but to have had good teachers at home, and to have learned that on such things one should spend without grudging the cost.
5. From my tutor: not to have taken sides with the Greens or the Blues at the races, nor with the light-shield or the heavy-shield men in the ring; to endure hardship and to want little; to work with my own hands, and to mind my own affairs; and to turn a deaf ear to slander.
6. From Diognetus: to avoid empty enthusiasms; to disbelieve what the miracle-mongers and charlatans say about spells and the casting-out of spirits and suchlike; not to breed fighting-quails, nor to be carried away by such pastimes; to tolerate plain speaking; to have grown intimate with philosophy, and to have heard first Bacchius, then Tandasis and Marcianus; to have written dialogues as a boy; and to have set my heart on the plank bed and the hide coverlet, and the rest of the discipline that belongs to the Greek training.
7. From Rusticus: to have grasped that my character stood in need of correction and care; not to be sidetracked into the ambition of the sophist, nor to write treatises on abstract questions, nor to deliver little moralizing addresses, nor to parade myself as a man of discipline or of good works; to have given up rhetoric and poetry and fine phrasing; not to walk about the house in formal robes, nor do anything of the kind; to write letters plainly, as he himself wrote to my mother from Sinuessa; to be easily won back to good will and readily reconciled with those who have given offence or done me wrong, the moment they themselves are willing to return; to read closely, and not be satisfied with a rough general grasp, nor agree too quickly with the glib talker; and to have come upon the memoirs of Epictetus, which he lent me from his own library.
8. From Apollonius: freedom of will, and an unwavering steadiness that leaves nothing to chance; to look to nothing else, even for a moment, but reason; to be ever the same — in sharp pain, at the loss of a child, through long illness; to see plainly, in a living example, that one and the same man can be both utterly resolute and at ease; not to be ill-tempered in explaining things; and to have seen a man who plainly counted as the least of his merits his experience and skill in handing on his teachings; and to have learned how one should receive what pass for favours from friends — neither enslaved by them nor letting them go unfelt.
9. From Sextus: graciousness; the model of a household governed as a father governs his own; the idea of living in accordance with nature; dignity without affectation; a watchful, caring attention to friends; patience with the unlearned and with those who hold opinions without examining them; an adaptability towards all men, so that his conversation was more winning than any flattery, and yet at that very moment he was held in the deepest reverence by those same men; the gift of finding out and arranging, with method and intelligence, the principles necessary for life; never to give a sign of anger or any other passion, but to be at once entirely free of passion and most affectionate; to bestow praise without fanfare, and to carry great learning without display.

title: Meditations
text:
10. From Alexander the grammarian: not to be fault-finding, nor to pounce reproachfully on those who let slip a barbarism, a solecism, or a harsh-sounding phrase, but deftly to introduce the very expression that should have been used, by way of an answer, a confirmation, or a shared reflection on the matter itself — not on the word — or by some other graceful, indirect reminder.
11. From Fronto: to mark what envy, duplicity, and hypocrisy go hand in hand with absolute power, and how those among us who are called patricians are somehow rather wanting in natural affection.
12. From Alexander the Platonist: not often, and never without necessity, to say to anyone, or write in a letter, that I am too busy; nor in this way to be forever begging off the duties I owe to those who share my life, pleading the press of affairs.
13. From Catulus: not to make light of a friend's complaint, even when it happens to be unreasonable, but to try to restore him to his usual temper; to speak warmly in praise of one's teachers, as Domitius and Athenodotus are remembered to have done; and a genuine love towards one's children.
14. From my brother Severus: love of family, of truth, and of justice; that through him I came to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus, and conceived the idea of a commonwealth under equal laws, governed by equality and freedom of speech, and of a kingship that honours above all else the liberty of the governed. And further, from him: a steady and even regard for philosophy; readiness to do good and to give without stint; good hope, and confidence in being loved by one's friends; openness towards those he found at fault; and that his friends had no need to guess at what he wished or did not wish — it was plain to see.
15. From Maximus: mastery of oneself, swayed by nothing; good cheer in all circumstances, and in sickness too; a character finely tempered — gentle and dignified together; to do the work set before him without complaint; that all men believed he thought as he spoke, and that whatever he did, he did with no ill intent. Never to be astonished or dismayed; never hurried, never hesitant, never at a loss, never downcast, never with a forced smile, and again never angry or suspicious; to be generous in kindness, ready to forgive, free of falsehood; to give the impression of a man who could not be bent from the straight path rather than one straightened by another; and that no one could ever have thought himself looked down on by him, nor have dared to suppose himself the better man; and a charm in good humour.
16. From my father: gentleness, and an unshakeable constancy in decisions reached after due examination; no vanity in the matter of so-called honours; love of work, and perseverance; a readiness to listen to anyone with something to contribute for the common good; an unswerving will to give every man his due; the experience to know where to press hard and where to ease off; and the putting away of the passion for boys. His sense of fellowship; and that he let his friends feel under no obligation always to dine with him or to attend him on his journeys, so that those kept away by some necessity always found him unchanged. His careful, persevering spirit in council, never breaking off an inquiry content with first impressions. His way of keeping his friends, never tiring of them nor doting on them. Self-sufficiency in everything, and a cheerful face. To look far ahead, and to arrange even the smallest matters in advance, without making a scene of it. To check, in his own case, all public acclamation and flattery. To watch ceaselessly over the needs of the empire, to husband its resources, and to bear the criticism that came of such care. Neither superstitious before the gods, nor, with men, a courter of the crowd, an ingratiating flatterer of the mob, but sober in all things and steadfast, nowhere vulgar nor chasing after novelty. In the things that make life comfortable — of which fortune gave him an abundance — to make use of them without display and without apology, so that when they were at hand he enjoyed them without affectation, and when they were absent he did not feel their lack. That no one could call him a sophist, a glib upstart, or a pedant, but rather a man ripe and complete, beyond the reach of flattery, fit to govern his own affairs and other men's. Besides this, his respect for the true followers of philosophy, while towards the rest he was neither scornful nor easily led astray by them. His ease and grace in company, never to the point of excess. His care for his own body within measure — not as one in love with life, nor for the sake of appearance, yet not negligently either, but so that, by his own attention, he had the least possible need of medicine, of drugs, or of outward remedies. Above all, his readiness to give way, without a trace of envy, to those who had gained some special competence — in eloquence, say, or the knowledge of laws or customs or other matters — and his eagerness to help them, so that each might win the repute his own gifts deserved. Acting always according to the ways of our fathers, yet not making even this — the keeping of ancestral custom — a thing to be seen doing. Not given to change or restlessness, but content to linger in the same places and at the same tasks; and, after his bouts of headache, returning at once fresh and vigorous to his usual work. His secrets were few — very few, and very rare, and those only on matters of state. Discretion and moderation in mounting public shows, in the building of public works, in distributions to the people, and the like — the conduct of a man who looks to what must be done, not to the reputation that follows the doing. He was no bather at odd hours, no lover of building, no connoisseur of his food, of the weave and colour of his clothes, or of the bloom of young bodies. His dress was brought up from his country house at Lorium; at Lanuvium he lived for the most part simply; we recall how he treated the customs-officer who begged his pardon at Tusculum, and all his behaviour was of that kind. There was nothing harsh in him, nothing relentless, nothing headlong — nothing of which one might say "he is sweating at it" — but everything was reasoned out separately, as if at leisure: untroubled, orderly, vigorous, and all of a piece with itself. What is recorded of Socrates would fit him too: that he could equally abstain from, and enjoy, those things which most men are too weak to abstain from and too self-indulgent to enjoy in moderation. But to be strong enough for the one and sober enough for the other is the mark of a man whose soul is perfect and unconquered — as he showed in the illness of Maximus.

title: Meditations
text:
17. From the gods: to have had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good companions, kinsmen, and friends — very nearly all of them good; and that I never stumbled into giving offence to any of them, though I had a disposition such that, given the occasion, I might have done something of the kind — but it was the gods' kindness that no concurrence of circumstances arose to put me to the test. That I was not reared longer than I was in my grandfather's concubine's house; that I kept the flower of my youth; that I did not prove my manhood before the time, but even held off a while longer. That I was set under a ruler and a father who would strip me of all conceit and bring me to see that one may live in a palace and yet have no need of bodyguards, of splendid robes, of torches and statues and pomp of that kind, but may draw oneself in very near to the condition of a private man, and be none the meaner or more remiss for it in whatever must be done, as a sovereign, for the common good. That I was granted such a brother — one able by his character to rouse me to care for myself, and at the same time gladdening me with his respect and affection. That my children were not born dull, nor deformed in body. That I made no great progress in rhetoric and poetry and the other pursuits in which I might well have been caught up, had I felt myself getting on easily. That I was quick to set my tutors in the positions of honour they seemed to long for, and did not put them off with the hope of doing it later, since they were still young. That I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus. That it was brought home to me clearly and often what a life in accordance with nature is, so that, as far as the gods are concerned, and the gifts, the help, and the inspirations that come from them, nothing now prevents me from living in accordance with nature — though I still fall short of it through my own fault, and through not keeping in mind the reminders, almost the instructions, of the gods. That my body has held out so long in such a life. That I never laid a hand on Benedicta or Theodotus, and that, when later I was caught up in passions of love, I was cured. That, though often angry with Rusticus, I never went so far as to do anything I would have regretted. That my mother, though fated to die young, yet spent her last years with me. That whenever I wished to help anyone in poverty or other need, I was never told there were no funds for it; and that I myself never fell into the like need of having to take from another. That my wife is what she is — so obedient, so affectionate, so unaffected. That I had no lack of suitable tutors for my children. That remedies were granted me through dreams — among others, against the spitting of blood and against dizziness; and what happened at Caieta, "as you shall use it." That, when I set my heart on philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor sit down to pore over treatises, or unravel syllogisms, or busy myself with the phenomena of the heavens. For all these things "stand in need of the gods' help, and of fortune."
*Among the Quadi, on the Granua.*
1. Say to yourself at daybreak: today I shall meet with the meddler, the ingrate, the bully, the schemer, the envious, the unsociable. All this has befallen them through ignorance of good and evil. But I, who have seen that the nature of the good is what is noble, and the nature of evil what is base, and that the nature of the wrongdoer himself is akin to mine — not of the same blood or seed, but sharing in the same mind and the same portion of the divine — I can be harmed by none of them, for none can fasten on me anything base; nor can I be angry with my kinsman, or hate him. We were born to work together, like the feet, the hands, the eyelids, like the rows of upper and lower teeth. To work against one another, then, is against nature; and to be vexed with a man and turn away from him is to work against him.

title: Meditations
text:
2. Whatever this thing is that I am, it is a little flesh, a little breath, and the ruling faculty. Put away your books; be distracted no longer; that is not granted you. Rather, as one already dying, despise the flesh: it is gore and bones and a flimsy web, a network woven of nerves, little veins, and arteries. Consider too what the breath is: wind, and never the same, but disgorged and gulped in again at every hour. The third thing, then, is the ruling faculty. Reflect thus: you are an old man; do not let this any longer be a slave, no longer be jerked like a puppet by impulses that serve no fellowship, no longer chafe at your present lot or shrink from what is to come.
3. The works of the gods are full of providence. The works of fortune are not apart from nature, nor from the spinning and weaving together of the things ordained by providence. From there all things flow; and joined to it are necessity and the good of the whole universe, of which you are a part. And to every part of nature that is good which the Nature of the Whole brings, and which preserves that nature. Now the universe is preserved by the changes of the elements, and likewise by the changes of the bodies compounded of them. Let these things suffice you; hold them as your settled principles. But cast away your thirst for books, that you may not die murmuring, but truly serene, and from the heart thankful to the gods.
4. Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how often, after receiving from the gods your appointed days, you have not used them. Now at last you must perceive of what universe you are a part, and from what governor of the universe you came forth as an emanation; and that a limit of your time is set, which, if you do not use it to clear your skies, will be gone, and you will be gone, and it will never return.
5. At every hour give your whole attention, as a Roman and a man, to doing what is in hand with strict and unfeigned dignity, with affection, freedom, and justice, and to making yourself free from all other impressions. And you will make yourself free if you perform each act as though it were the last of your life, rid of all aimlessness and of any passionate turning away from the rule of reason, of all pretence, self-love, and discontent with what is allotted to you. You see how few are the things a man must master to live a life that flows easily and reverently; for the gods will ask nothing more of him who keeps to these.
6. Do violence to yourself, do violence to yourself, my soul; the time to honour yourself you will not have again. For each of us has but one life, and yours is nearly spent, and yet you have no respect for yourself, but make your own welfare depend on the souls of others.
7. Do things from outside break in upon you and distract you? Then make yourself the leisure to learn something further that is good, and stop being carried this way and that. But there is another straying to be guarded against as well: for those are foolish too who have worn themselves out with activity in life and yet have no goal toward which to direct every impulse and, in a word, every impression.
8. A man is rarely seen to be unhappy for failing to attend to what passes in another's soul; but those who do not closely follow the movements of their own soul must of necessity be unhappy.
9. These things you must always bear in mind: what the Nature of the Whole is, and what my own nature is, and how this stands toward that, and what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that no one can prevent you from always acting and speaking in accordance with the nature of which you are a part.

title: Meditations
text:
10. Theophrastus speaks like a philosopher when, in comparing offences — as one might compare such things on the common view — he says that the faults committed through desire are graver than those committed through anger. For the angry man seems to turn from reason with a certain pain and a hidden contraction of the soul; but he who sins through desire, being overcome by pleasure, shows himself somehow more unrestrained and more unmanly in his wrongdoing. Rightly, then, and in a manner worthy of philosophy, he said that the fault committed with pleasure deserves a heavier charge than the one committed with pain. And, on the whole, the one is more like a man first wronged and driven by pain to anger, while the other has of his own accord set out toward wrongdoing, carried by desire to do the deed.
11. Act, speak, and think in everything as one who could depart from life this very moment. But to go away from among men, if there are gods, is nothing to dread; for they would not involve you in evil. And if there are no gods, or if they take no care for human affairs, why should I wish to live in a universe empty of gods, empty of providence? But there are gods, and they do care for human affairs; and they have put it wholly in man's own power not to fall into things that are truly evil. And as for the rest, had any of it been evil, they would have provided against that too, so that it should lie within every man's power not to fall into it. But how could that which does not make a man worse make his life worse? The Nature of the Whole would not have overlooked these things, neither through ignorance, nor knowing them yet unable to guard against or correct them; nor would it have erred so greatly, whether through want of power or want of skill, as to let good and evil befall good and bad men alike, at random. Now death and life, fame and obscurity, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty — all these befall good and bad men alike, being neither noble nor base. They are therefore neither good nor evil.
12. How swiftly all things vanish — in the universe the bodies themselves, and in time the memory of them. Such are all the objects of sense, and most of all those that lure us with pleasure, or frighten us with pain, or are trumpeted abroad through vanity: how cheap, how contemptible, how sordid, how perishable and dead they are — these the intellectual faculty must mark. And what are these men whose opinions and voices bestow good repute? What is it to die; and that, if a man looks at it alone, and by dividing it in thought strips away the fancies that gather about it, he will think it nothing else than a work of nature — and whoever fears a work of nature is a child. Yet this is not only a work of nature, but also profitable to her. And how man touches God, and by what part of himself, and how that part of man must be disposed.
13. Nothing is more wretched than the man who goes round and round over everything, and "searches into the things beneath the earth," as the poet says, and seeks by conjecture into the souls of those about him, while failing to perceive that it is enough to keep close to the guardian spirit within him and to serve it sincerely. And to serve it is to keep it pure of passion, of aimlessness, and of discontent with whatever comes from gods and from men. For what comes from the gods is to be revered for its excellence; and what comes from men is dear to us through kinship, and at times in a manner pitiable through their ignorance of good and evil — a maiming no less grave than that which robs the eyes of the power to tell white from black.

title: Meditations
text:
14. Though you were to live three thousand years, or ten times as many, still remember that no man loses any other life than the one he is living, nor lives any other than the one he loses. The longest life, then, and the shortest come to the same. For the present moment is equal for all, and so what is being lost is equal, and what is taken from a man is shown to be the merest instant. For no one can lose either the past or the future; how can anyone be robbed of what he does not possess? Two things, then, must be remembered: first, that all things from everlasting are of one kind and run in cycles, and it makes no difference whether one shall see the same things for a hundred years, or two hundred, or through endless time; second, that the longest-lived and the soonest to die lose the same. For the present is the only thing of which a man can be deprived, since this is all he has; and what a man does not have, he cannot lose.
15. That all is opinion. Plain enough are the sayings addressed to Monimus the Cynic; and plain too is their usefulness, if one takes the pith of the saying so far as it is true.
16. The soul of man does violence to itself, first and chiefly when it becomes, so far as it can, an abscess and, as it were, a tumour upon the universe; for to chafe at anything that happens is to set oneself apart from Nature, in whose embrace the several natures of all other things are contained. Next, when it turns away from any man, or is borne against him to do him harm, as are the souls of the angry. Third, it does violence to itself when it is overcome by pleasure or by pain. Fourth, when it plays a part, and does or says anything feigned and untruthful. Fifth, when it lets some action of its own and some impulse go without an aim, but acts at random and unreflectingly, when even the smallest acts ought to be done with reference to the end. And the end of rational beings is to follow the reason and ordinance of that most venerable city and commonwealth.
17. Of human life, the time is a point, the substance flowing, the perception dim, the composition of the whole body quick to rot, the soul a whirligig, fortune hard to foretell, and fame a thing past all judging. In a word, all that belongs to the body is a river, and all that belongs to the soul is dream and vapour; life is a war and a sojourn in a strange land, and the fame that comes after is forgetting. What, then, can see us through? One thing and one alone: philosophy. And this lies in keeping the guardian spirit within free from outrage and unhurt, master of pleasures and pains, doing nothing at random, nothing falsely or with pretence, having no need of another's doing or not doing anything; and, further, in welcoming what befalls and is allotted as coming from that source from which it came itself; and, above all, in awaiting death with a serene mind, as nothing but a dissolution of the elements of which every living creature is composed. But if it is no terror to the elements themselves that each is continually changing into another, why should one look with suspicion on the change and dissolution of all things? For it is in accordance with nature; and nothing that is in accordance with nature is evil.
*Written at Carnuntum.*
1. We must reckon not only that life is being spent day by day, and an ever smaller part of it left; but this too must be reckoned, that even if a man should live longer, it is uncertain whether the understanding will hold out as before, equal to the grasp of affairs and to that contemplation which strives after experience of things divine and human. For if a man begins to fail in mind, breathing and nourishment, the play of impressions and the working of impulse, and all such things, will not give out; but the power to use oneself, to mark with precision the measure of one's duty, to set in order what is presented to the mind, to consider whether the time has come to take oneself off — all that calls for a thoroughly trained reason — is quenched before the rest. We must press on, then, not only because we draw nearer to death at every moment, but also because the comprehension of things and the close attention to them flag and fail before the end.

title: Meditations
text:
2. We must also note that even the by-products of things produced by nature have a certain grace and charm. When a loaf is baked, some parts split open; and these cracks, which thus gape and in a way run counter to the baker's intent, have a certain fitness of their own, and stir the appetite for food in a peculiar way. Figs, again, gape widest when at their ripest; and in olives ripened on the tree, the very nearness of decay lends a peculiar beauty to the fruit. The ears of corn bending earthward, the lion's lowering brow, the foam streaming from the wild boar's jaws, and many other things — if one were to look at them by themselves, far from comely — yet, because they follow upon the works of nature, lend a further grace and please the soul. So that if a man has feeling and a deeper insight into the things that come to pass in the whole, there is scarcely one of them, even among the things that happen by way of consequence, that will not seem to him in some way pleasingly disposed. Such a man will look on the real gaping jaws of wild beasts with no less pleasure than on those that painters and sculptors set before us in imitation; and in the old woman and the old man he will be able to see a certain ripeness and bloom, and the loveliness of children, with his own chaste eyes. And many such things will come home, not to everyone, but only to him who has grown genuinely intimate with Nature and her works.
3. Hippocrates, after curing many diseases, himself fell sick and died. The Chaldeans foretold the deaths of many men, and then their own appointed fate overtook them too. Alexander, Pompey, and Gaius Caesar, after so often razing whole cities to the ground and cutting down in pitched battle myriads of horse and foot, themselves at last departed from life. Heraclitus, after all his speculations on the conflagration of the universe, was filled within with water, plastered over with cow-dung, and so died. Vermin destroyed Democritus, and other vermin Socrates. What of it? You embarked, you sailed, you have come to port: step ashore. If it is to another life, there is no place empty of gods, not even there; and if to insensibility, you will cease to endure pains and pleasures and to be a slave to a vessel as much meaner than that which serves it — for the one is mind and guardian spirit, the other earth and gore.
4. Do not waste the part of life that is left in imaginings about other men, except when you direct them to some common good; for so you rob yourself of other work. That is, by picturing what so-and-so is doing, and why, and what he says, and what he is plotting, and all such things, you are made to wander from the watch over your own ruling faculty. We must, then, banish from the train of our impressions all that is aimless and idle, and most of all the meddlesome and malicious; and we must train ourselves to imagine only those things about which, if a man were suddenly to ask, "What are you thinking of now?", we could at once answer with frankness, "This and that" — so that from the answer it would be plain at once that all is simple and kindly, the thought of a being made for fellowship, one who cares nothing for the imaginings of pleasure or of indulgence generally, or for rivalry, or envy, or suspicion, or anything else that one would blush to own one had in mind. For such a man, no longer putting off the day, is even now among the best; he is a kind of priest and minister of the gods, employing also that which is seated within him, which keeps a man unstained by pleasures, unwounded by any pain, untouched by any outrage, insensible to all wickedness — an athlete in the greatest of contests, that of being thrown by no passion; dyed deep in justice; welcoming with his whole soul all that befalls and is allotted to him; not often, and never without some great and common need, imagining what another may be saying or doing or thinking. For he has only his own concerns to work upon, and he reflects continually on what is spun for him out of the whole; and the former he keeps fair, while of the latter he is persuaded that they are good. For the lot assigned to each is carried along with the whole, and carries the whole along with it. And he remembers, too, that all rational beings are kin, and that to care for all men is according to the nature of man; that one must hold fast, not to the opinion of all men, but only of those who live in agreement with nature. As for those who do not so live, he keeps ever in mind what manner of men they are, at home and abroad, by night and by day, and with what manner of company they herd. He sets no store, therefore, by the praise of such men, who do not even please themselves.

title: Meditations
text:
5. Act neither unwillingly, nor selfishly, nor without examination, nor against your own better judgment. Let no studied elegance dress up your thought. Be neither a great talker nor a busybody. Further, let the god within you be the guardian of a being that is male, mature, devoted to the commonwealth, a Roman and a ruler, who has taken his post like one awaiting the recall from life, ready to march off, needing neither oath nor any man for witness. And let there be in you cheerfulness, and no need of help from outside, nor of the peace that others give. You must stand upright, then, not be held upright by others.
6. If in human life you can find anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage — than your understanding, in a word, content with itself in the things wherein it makes you act according to right reason, and content with its lot in what is allotted to you apart from your choice — if, I say, you can see anything better than this, then turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy this best thing that you have found. But if nothing shows itself better than the very divinity seated within you, which has brought your own impulses under its sway, which scrutinizes your impressions, which has withdrawn itself, as Socrates said, from the persuasions of the senses, and has made itself subject to the gods and careful of men — if you find all else smaller and cheaper than this, then give place to nothing else; for once you have inclined and turned aside toward any other thing, you will no longer be able, without distraction, to give the first honour to that good which is your own and proper to you. For it is not lawful that anything of a different kind should be set up as a rival to the good of reason and fellowship — neither the praise of the many, nor offices, nor wealth, nor the enjoyment of pleasures. All these things, even if they seem to fit for a little while, suddenly master a man and carry him off. But do you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold fast to it. "And the better is what profits." If it profits you as a rational being, keep to it; but if only as an animal, say so plainly, and guard your judgment without conceit; only see that you make the inquiry surely.
7. Never value as profitable to yourself anything that will compel you one day to break your faith, to abandon your sense of honour, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play the hypocrite, to long for anything that needs walls and curtains to hide it. For the man who has set above all else his own mind and guardian spirit and the rites of its virtue makes no tragedy of life, utters no groans, and will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Above all, he will live neither pursuing nor fleeing; and whether for a longer span of time or a shorter he is to use his soul enclosed in the body matters to him not at all. For even if he must depart this moment, he will go as readily as he would do any other thing that can be done with decency and order, taking care throughout his whole life of this one thing only: that his understanding be never turned to anything unbecoming a rational and social being.
8. In the mind of the man who has been chastened and purified you would find nothing festering, nothing soiled, nothing rankling beneath the surface; nor does his appointed fate overtake his life unfinished, as one might say of an actor leaving the stage before he has played out his part and completed the drama. Moreover, you would find in him nothing servile, nothing showy, nothing too tightly bound or too sharply cut off, nothing to answer for, nothing skulking in a corner.

title: Meditations
text:
9. Reverence the power of forming opinions. On this everything depends, that no opinion may arise in your ruling faculty out of keeping with nature and with the constitution of a rational being. And this constitution promises freedom from rashness, kinship with men, and obedience to the gods.
10. Cast away all else, then, and hold fast to these few things alone. Remember besides that each man lives only this present, the fleeting instant; the rest has either been lived already or lies in uncertainty. Little, then, is the span each man lives; little the corner of the earth where he lives; and little, too, the longest fame thereafter — and even that handed on through a succession of poor mortals very soon to die, who do not know even themselves, far less one long dead.
11. To the principles already named let one more be added: always to make a definition or sketch of the object presented to the imagination, so as to see it as it is in its essence, naked, whole, and divided into its parts, and to name to oneself both its own name and the names of those things out of which it is compounded and into which it will be dissolved. For nothing is so apt to produce greatness of mind as the power to examine, by method and in truth, each of the things that meet us in life, and always so to look at them as to consider at the same time what sort of universe this is, what use the thing serves in it, what worth it has in relation to the whole and what in relation to man, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which all other cities are as households. What is this that now produces an impression in me? Of what is it composed? How long is it of its nature to last? And what virtue does it call for in dealing with it — gentleness, courage, good faith, simplicity, self-sufficiency, and the rest? Therefore in each case one must say: this comes from God; this comes by the allotment, the woven web of destiny, and such concurrence and chance; and this comes from my fellow, my kinsman and partner, who is ignorant, however, of what is according to his nature. But I am not ignorant; and therefore I treat him, according to the natural law of fellowship, with good will and justice, while at the same time, in matters indifferent, I aim at his deserts.
12. If you do the present task following right reason, earnestly, vigorously, kindly, allowing no by-end to creep in, but keeping the guardian spirit within you pure, as though even now you had to give it back; if you join this to the present, expecting nothing and shunning nothing, content with present action according to nature and with the heroic truth of all you say and utter — then you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.
13. As physicians always keep their instruments and knives ready to hand for sudden cases, so do you keep your principles ready for the knowledge of things divine and human, and do even the smallest thing as one mindful of the bond that binds the two together. For you will do nothing well in human affairs without referring it also to the divine, nor anything divine without referring it to the human.
14. No longer wander from your course; for you are not going to read your own notes, nor the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks, nor those extracts from books that you laid up for your old age. Press on, then, to the end, and, casting away empty hopes, come to your own aid, while it is still in your power, if you have any care for yourself.
15. They do not know how many things are meant by "to steal," "to sow," "to buy," "to keep quiet," "to see what must be done" — which last is the work, not of the eyes, but of another kind of sight.

title: Meditations
text:
16. Body, soul, mind: to the body belong the senses, to the soul the impulses, to the mind the principles. To receive impressions through the imagination belongs even to cattle; to be jerked by impulses like a puppet belongs even to wild beasts, to the unmanly, to a Phalaris and a Nero. To have the mind as guide toward what appears to be one's duty belongs even to those who do not believe in the gods, who betray their country, and who do anything once they have shut their doors. If, then, all else is shared with the men just named, what remains as proper to the good man is this: to love and welcome what befalls and is woven into the web of his fate, and not to defile or trouble with a throng of impressions the guardian spirit seated within his breast, but to keep it serene, following the god in good order, speaking nothing contrary to truth, doing nothing contrary to justice. And if all men disbelieve that he lives simply, modestly, and cheerfully, he is angry with none of them, nor does he turn aside from the road that leads to the end of life, to which he must come pure, at peace, ready to depart, fitted without constraint to his own lot.
1. The ruling power within, when it is in accordance with nature, stands toward whatever befalls in such a way that it can always adapt itself easily to what is possible and granted. For it has no fondness for any particular material, but moves toward its chief ends with a reservation, and makes whatever crosses it into material for itself; just as fire, when it masters the things that fall into it, by which a little lamp would have been put out — the bright fire very swiftly appropriates to itself what is heaped upon it, consumes it, and from those very things rises higher.
2. Let no act be done at random, nor otherwise than according to a principle that fulfils the art.
3. Men seek retreats for themselves — country places, beaches, hills; and you too are wont to long for such things above all. But this is the mark of the most ordinary man, since it is in your power, whenever you wish, to retreat into yourself. For nowhere can a man retreat more quietly or more free of trouble than into his own soul, especially one who has within such things that, by looking into them, he is at once wholly at ease; and by ease I mean nothing but good order. Give yourself, then, continually this retreat, and renew yourself. But let your maxims be brief and elemental, such as, meeting you at once, will suffice to wash away all distress and to send you back without resentment to the things you return to. For what is it that vexes you? The wickedness of men? Recall the judgment that rational beings are made for one another, that to bear with them is part of justice, that they do wrong unwillingly, and how many, after their feuds, suspicions, hatreds, and battles, now lie stretched out and turned to ashes — and cease at last. But are you vexed too with what is allotted to you out of the whole? Then recall the alternative: either providence or atoms; and from how much it has been shown that the universe is, as it were, a city. But will bodily things still take hold of you? Then consider that the mind, once it has taken possession of itself and come to know its own power, does not mingle with the breath, whether it moves smoothly or roughly; and consider, too, all that you have heard and assented to concerning pain and pleasure. But will the desire for a little fame distract you? Then look at the swiftness with which all things are forgotten, at the chaos of infinite time on either hand, at the emptiness of applause, the fickleness and the want of judgment in those who seem to praise, and the narrowness of the space in which it is confined. For the whole earth is a mere point, and of this how tiny a corner is your dwelling-place; and here, how many will there be to praise you, and what manner of men? Remember, then, this withdrawal into your own little field, and above all do not strain or force yourself, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. And among the maxims most ready to hand, into which you will look, let these two be: first, that things do not touch the soul, but stand outside it unmoved, and our troubles come from the opinion within us alone; second, that all these things you see will in a moment change and be no more — and dwell continually on how many changes you yourself have already witnessed. The universe is alteration; life is opinion.

title: Meditations
text:
4. If the intellectual faculty is common to us, then so too is the reason by which we are rational; if so, then that reason also is common which commands what is to be done or not done; if so, then law also is common; if so, then we are fellow citizens; if so, then we share in a commonwealth; if so, then the universe is, as it were, a city. For of what other common commonwealth will anyone say that the whole race of men shares? And from there, from this common city, comes the very faculty that is intellectual, rational, and law-abiding in us — or from where else? For just as the earthy part in me has been apportioned from some earth, the watery from another element, the breath from some source, and the hot and fiery from some source of its own — since nothing comes from nothing, just as nothing departs into nothing — so too the intellectual part has come from somewhere.
5. Death, like birth, is a mystery of nature: a combining of the same elements, and a dissolving into the same. It is altogether nothing to be ashamed of; for it is not contrary to the order of a rational being, nor against the reason of its constitution.
6. These things are bound by their nature to come from such men by necessity; and he who would not have it so would have the fig-tree yield no juice. And in any case remember this: that within a very little while both you and he will be dead, and soon after not even your name will be left.
7. Take away the opinion, and the "I have been harmed" is taken away; take away the "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
8. What does not make a man himself worse does not make his life worse either, nor does it harm him from without or from within.
9. The nature of what is beneficial has been compelled to do this.
10. That "everything that happens, happens justly" — which, if you watch closely, you will find to be so; I mean not merely in the order of sequence, but in accordance with justice, and as if by one who apportions according to desert. Watch closely, then, as you have begun, and whatever you do, do it together with this: with being good, in the sense in which the good man is properly understood. Keep this in every act.
11. Do not take things to be such as the man who insults you judges them, or wishes you to judge them; but see them as they are in truth.
12. These two readinesses one must always have: the one, to do only what the reason of the kingly and law-giving faculty suggests for the benefit of men; the other, to change one's course if someone is at hand to correct and turn one aside from some opinion. But the turning aside must always come from some persuasion of justice or common good, and the things preferred must be such only for that reason, and not because they appeared pleasant or won esteem.
13. "Have you reason?" "I have." "Why then do you not use it? For if it does its own work, what more do you want?"
14. You have come into being as a part; you will vanish into that which gave you birth — or rather, you will be taken up again, through change, into its generative reason.
15. Many grains of incense fall on the same altar; one falls first, another later, but it makes no difference.
16. Within ten days you will seem a god to the very men to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you return to your principles and to the reverence of reason.
17. Do not act as though you had ten thousand years to live. The inevitable hangs over you. While you live, while it is in your power, be good.
18. How much leisure he gains who does not look at what his neighbour said or did or intended, but only at what he himself does, that it may be just and holy — or, as the good man does, who does not gaze about at the dark character of others, but runs straight along the line, without swerving.

title: Meditations
text:
19. The man who is in a flutter about fame hereafter does not picture to himself that each of those who remember him will himself very soon die, and then in turn the one who succeeded him, until all memory is quenched, passing on through men who are kindled and put out. But suppose that those who will remember are immortal, and the memory immortal: what is that to you? And I do not say merely that it is nothing to the dead; but to the living, what is praise, except for some practical use? For you are now putting off, out of season, the gift of nature, and clinging instead to some other consideration.
20. Everything that is in any way beautiful is beautiful of itself, and ends in itself, having praise as no part of it; for the thing praised is made neither worse nor better by it. This I say also of the things commonly called beautiful — material things and works of art. As for that which is truly beautiful, what need has it of anything beyond? No more than law, no more than truth, no more than kindness or modesty. Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or marred because it is blamed? Does an emerald become worse than itself if it is not praised? And what of gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a little knife, a flower, a little shrub?
21. If souls continue to exist, how does the air contain them from all eternity? And how does the earth contain the bodies of those buried for so long an age? For just as here the change and dissolution of these bodies, after they have lasted a certain time, makes room for other corpses, so the souls that pass into the air, after enduring for a time, change and are diffused and kindled into flame, taken up again into the generative reason of the whole, and in this way make room for those who come to dwell beside them. This is what one might answer, on the supposition that souls continue to exist. But one must consider not only the multitude of bodies thus buried, but also that of the living creatures eaten each day by us and by the other animals. For what a number is consumed and, in a manner, buried in the bodies of those who feed on them; and yet the place receives them, through their being turned to blood, through their alteration into air or fire. What, in this matter, is the way to truth? Division into the material and the causal.
22. Do not be carried this way and that, but in every impulse render what is just, and in every impression preserve the power of clear comprehension.
23. All that is in tune with you is in tune with me, O Universe; nothing is too early or too late for me that is timely for you. All is fruit for me that your seasons bring, O Nature; from you are all things, in you are all things, to you return all things. The poet says, "Dear city of Cecrops"; will you not say, "Dear city of Zeus"?
24. "Do few things," he says, "if you would have peace of mind." But is it not better to do the necessary things, and only what the reason of a creature made for fellowship requires, and as it requires? For this brings not only the peace that comes from doing well, but also the peace that comes from doing few things. For if a man strips away the greater part of what we say and do, being unnecessary, he will have more leisure and less disturbance. Therefore on each occasion one should remind oneself: is this one of the unnecessary things? And one must strip away not only unnecessary acts, but unnecessary impressions as well; for so no superfluous acts will follow either.
25. Try how the life of the good man also suits you — the man content with what is allotted to him out of the whole, and satisfied with his own just conduct and kindly disposition.

title: Meditations
text:
26. You have seen those things; now look at these. Do not trouble yourself; make yourself simple. Does someone do wrong? He does wrong to himself. Has something befallen you? Good; it was woven for you out of the whole from the beginning, and spun together with your fate, all that befalls. In sum, life is short; gain from the present moment by good sense and justice. Be sober, but at ease.
27. Either an ordered universe, or a medley jumbled together but still a universe. Or can there be order subsisting within you, while in the whole there is disorder? And this when all things are so distinguished, so interfused, and so bound by sympathy.
28. A black character, a womanish character, a stubborn character, bestial, brutish, childish, dull, counterfeit, buffoonish, hucksterish, tyrannical.
29. If he is a stranger to the universe who does not recognize the things that are in it, no less a stranger is he who does not recognize the things that come to pass in it. He is a runaway who flees the reason of the commonwealth; blind, who shuts the eye of the mind; a beggar, who has need of another and does not have within himself all that is useful for life. He is an abscess on the universe who withdraws and cuts himself off from the reason of our common nature through discontent with what befalls; for that same nature brings this to pass, which also brought you forth. He is a fragment torn from the city who tears his own soul away from the soul of rational beings, which is one.
30. One man philosophizes without a tunic, another without a book. Here is one half-naked: "I have no bread," he says, "and yet I hold fast to reason." And I have not the nourishment that comes of learning, and yet I hold fast.
31. Love the modest craft you have learned, and rest in it; and pass through the remainder of your life as one who has entrusted all that is his to the gods with his whole soul, making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any man.
32. Consider, for example, the times of Vespasian: you will see all the same things — men marrying, raising children, falling sick, dying, making war, keeping festivals, trading, farming, flattering, asserting themselves, suspecting, plotting, praying for the death of some, grumbling at the present, loving, hoarding, longing for consulships and kingdoms. And that life of theirs is now nowhere. Pass again to the times of Trajan: again all the same things; and that life too is dead. Likewise survey the other inscriptions of the ages, of whole nations, and see how many, after great straining, soon fell and were resolved into the elements. But above all you should recall those whom you yourself have known wasting their efforts on empty things, neglecting to do what their own constitution required, to cling fast to that and be content with it. And here it is needful to remember that the attention given to each action has its own proper worth and measure; for so you will not lose heart, if you do not busy yourself with lesser things beyond what is fitting.
33. The words once in common use are now archaic; so too the names of men once much sung are now in a way archaisms — Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Dentatus; and a little later Scipio and Cato, then Augustus too, then Hadrian and Antoninus. For all things fade and quickly become the stuff of legend, and quickly utter oblivion buries them. And this I say of those who shone in some wonderful way; for the rest, the moment they breathe their last, are "out of sight, out of mind." And what, in any case, is everlasting remembrance? Wholly empty. What, then, is the thing on which we should spend our care? This one thing: a just mind, and acts done for the common good, and speech that never lies, and a disposition that welcomes all that befalls as necessary, as familiar, as flowing from such a source and spring.

title: Meditations
text:
34. Of your own will give yourself up to Clotho, and let her spin you into whatever events she pleases.
35. All is of a day, both what remembers and what is remembered.
36. Observe continually that all things come to be by change, and accustom yourself to consider that the Nature of the Whole loves nothing so much as to change what exists and to make new things like them. For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will come to be from it; but you imagine that only those things are seeds which are cast into the earth or the womb — and that is very crude.
37. You will soon be dead, and you are still not simple, not untroubled, not free of the suspicion of being harmed from without, not gracious to all, nor placing wisdom solely in acting justly.
38. Look closely into their ruling faculties — even the wise — and see what they shun and what they pursue.
39. Your evil does not subsist in another's ruling faculty, nor indeed in any turn or alteration of your surroundings. Where, then? In that part of you which forms opinions about evils. Let it, then, not form such opinions, and all is well. And even if the body nearest to it is cut, burned, festers, rots, still let the part that forms opinions about these things keep quiet; that is, let it judge nothing to be either evil or good which can befall the bad man and the good alike. For what befalls alike the man who lives contrary to nature and the man who lives in accordance with nature is neither in accordance with nature nor contrary to it.
40. Conceive continually of the universe as one living being, holding one substance and one soul; and how all things are taken up into its single perception; and how it does all things by a single impulse; and how all things are joint causes of all that comes to be; and what manner of spinning and weaving together there is.
41. You are a little soul carrying a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.
42. There is no evil for things that are in process of change, just as there is no good for things that subsist out of change.
43. Time is a kind of river of the things that come to be, a violent stream; for no sooner is each thing seen than it has been swept by, and another is borne along, and that too will be swept away.
44. Everything that happens is as familiar and well known as the rose in spring and the fruit in summer; for such is disease, and death, and slander, and treachery, and all that gladdens or grieves fools.
45. The things that follow are always akin to those that went before; for it is not like a mere enumeration of separate items bound only by necessity, but a reasonable connection. And as existing things are arranged in harmony together, so the things that come to be display no bare succession, but a wonderful kinship.
46. Always remember the saying of Heraclitus, that the death of earth is to become water, the death of water to become air, of air fire, and back again. Remember too the man who forgets where the road leads; and that men are at variance with the very reason with which they most continually associate, the reason that governs all things; and that the things they meet with every day appear strange to them; and that we ought not to act and speak as men asleep — for even then we seem to act and speak; and that we ought not to act like children of our parents, that is, simply because we have received it so.
47. Just as, if one of the gods told you that you would die tomorrow, or at the latest the day after, you would make no great matter of the day after rather than tomorrow — unless you were utterly base; for how small is the interval? — so too think it no great thing to die after very many years rather than tomorrow.

title: Meditations
text:
48. Consider continually how many physicians have died, who often knit their brows over the sick; how many astrologers, after foretelling the deaths of others as something great; how many philosophers, after endless disputations about death or immortality; how many warriors, after slaying many men; how many tyrants, who used their power over lives with dreadful arrogance, as though they were immortal; and how many whole cities have died, if one may say so — Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and others without number. Go over, too, all whom you have known, one after another: this man, after burying that one, was then laid out himself; another buried him; and all in a short space. In a word, look always upon human things as fleeting and cheap: yesterday a little mucus, tomorrow a mummy or ashes. Pass, then, through this instant of time in accordance with nature, and lay down your life graciously, as an olive might fall when ripe, blessing the earth that bore it and giving thanks to the tree that brought it forth.
49. Be like the headland on which the waves break continually; it stands firm, and around it the boiling waters are laid to rest. "Unhappy am I, that this has befallen me." No: rather, "Happy am I, that, though this has befallen me, I continue free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor afraid of what is to come." For such a thing might have befallen anyone, but not everyone would have continued free from pain under it. Why then is that a misfortune, rather than this a good fortune? And do you call at all a misfortune for a man what is not a frustration of man's nature? And does that seem to you a frustration of man's nature which is not contrary to the will of his nature? What, then? You have learned that will. Does this that has befallen prevent you from being just, high-minded, temperate, sensible, free from rashness, free from deceit, modest, free, and the rest, in whose presence the nature of man attains what is its own? Remember, then, on every occasion that leads you toward grief, to use this maxim: this is no misfortune, but to bear it nobly is good fortune.
50. A homely yet effective help toward contempt of death is to run over those who have clung tenaciously to life. What more had they than those who died untimely? At all events, they lie somewhere — Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, or any such man, who carried out many to their graves and then were themselves carried out. In short, the interval is small, and that drawn out through how many troubles, in what company, in what a poor body. Do not, then, treat it as a great matter. For look behind you at the boundless gulf of time, and before you at another infinity. In this, what difference is there between him who lives three days and him who lives three generations?
51. Always run by the short road; and the short road is the natural one, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way. For such a purpose frees a man from toils, from contention, from all calculation and affectation.
1. At dawn, when you wake unwillingly, let this thought be ready to hand: I am rising to the work of a man. Why then am I out of humour, if I am going to do the things for which I was born, and for which I was brought into the world? Or was I framed for this, to lie warm under the blankets? "But this is more pleasant." Were you made, then, for pleasure — in short, to be acted upon, or to act? Do you not see the little plants, the sparrows, the ants, the spiders, the bees, each doing its own work, each helping in its way to set the universe in order? And you, will you not do the work of a man? Will you not run to that which is according to your nature? "But one must rest as well." One must, I grant; yet nature has set a measure to this, as she has set a measure to eating and drinking; and yet you go beyond the measure, beyond what suffices. In your actions, though, it is no longer so, but you stop short of what you can do. For you do not love yourself; if you did, you would love your nature too, and its will. Other men, who love their crafts, wear themselves out at their tasks, unwashed and unfed; but you honour your own nature less than the engraver honours his engraving, the dancer his dancing, the miser his money, the vainglorious man his little fame. These men, when the passion is on them, would rather not eat or sleep than fail to advance the things they care for; and to you do acts done for the common good seem cheaper, and worth less effort?

title: Meditations
text:
2. How easy it is to thrust away and blot out every disturbing or alien impression, and at once to be in perfect calm.
3. Judge yourself worthy of every word and deed that is in accordance with nature, and do not let the censure or the talk that follows from certain men distract you; but if it is good to be done or said, do not think yourself unworthy of it. For those men have their own ruling faculty and follow their own impulse; do not look round at these, but go straight on, following your own nature and the common nature; for the way of both is one.
4. I go forward through the things that are according to nature until I fall and have my rest, breathing out my last into that from which I daily draw breath, and falling upon that from which my father gathered the seed, my mother the blood, my nurse the milk; from which, all these years, I am fed and watered day by day; which bears me as I tread upon it and put it to so many uses.
5. They cannot admire you for sharpness of wit. Be it so; but there are many other qualities of which you cannot say, "It is not in my nature." Show forth, then, those that are wholly in your power: sincerity, dignity, endurance of toil, indifference to pleasure, contentment with your lot, the need of little, kindness, freedom, plainness, a freedom from idle talk, and largeness of mind. Do you not perceive how many things you are able even now to show forth, for which there is no excuse of natural incapacity or unfitness, and yet you still stay below of your own will? Or are you compelled, by some defect of nature, to grumble, to be grasping, to flatter, to lay the blame on your poor body, to play the toady, to brag, and to toss your soul about so? No, by the gods; you might have been rid of all this long since, and at most been convicted of being a little slow and dull of apprehension. Yet even this you must work at, neither neglecting it nor taking comfort in your sloth.
6. One man, when he has done another a good turn, is ready also to reckon it to him as a favour owed. Another is not so ready, but still in his own mind counts the man his debtor, and is conscious of what he has done. A third is in a manner not even conscious of what he has done, but is like a vine that has borne its grapes and seeks nothing further once it has yielded its proper fruit. As a horse runs, a hound tracks, a bee makes honey, so a man, when he has done a good deed, does not cry it abroad, but passes on to another, as the vine to bearing its grapes again in season. One must be, then, among those who do this in a manner without being conscious of it. "Yes, but one ought to be conscious of this very thing; for it is proper," they say, "to the man made for fellowship to perceive that he is acting for the fellowship, and, by Zeus, to wish his fellow to perceive it too." What you say is true, but you take the present saying amiss; and for this reason you will be one of those I mentioned before, for they too are led astray by a certain plausibility of reasoning. But if you are willing to understand what is meant, do not fear that you will on this account leave undone any work for the fellowship.
7. A prayer of the Athenians: "Rain, rain, dear Zeus, upon the ploughland of the Athenians and upon their plains." Either we should not pray at all, or we should pray thus, simply and freely.
8. Just as the saying goes, "Asclepius prescribed for this man horse-exercise, or cold baths, or going barefoot," so this too may be said: "The Nature of the Whole prescribed for this man disease, or maiming, or loss, or some such thing." For there "prescribed" means something like this: he ordained this for him as suited to his health; and here, what befalls each man has in some way been ordained for him as suited to his destiny. For we say that these things "befit" us, as the masons say that the squared stones in the walls or the pyramids "befit" one another, fitting together in a certain arrangement. For altogether there is one harmony; and just as out of all bodies the universe is made up into such a body, so out of all causes destiny is made up into such a cause. Even the most unlearned understand what I mean; for they say, "This was brought to him." Now if it was brought to him, then it was brought, and it was ordained for him; let us, then, receive these things as we receive what Asclepius ordains. Many of his prescriptions, indeed, are harsh, yet we welcome them in the hope of health. Let the accomplishment and fulfilment of what the common nature judges good seem to you of the same kind as your health; and so welcome all that comes to pass, even if it seem rather cruel, because it leads to that end, to the health of the universe and to the welfare and prosperity of Zeus. For he would not have brought this to anyone, if it were not of benefit to the whole; nor does any nature whatsoever bring anything that is not suited to that which it governs. On two grounds, then, you must love what befalls you: first, because it came to be for you, and was ordained for you, and stood in some relation to you, woven for you from the highest causes; second, because for him who governs the whole it is a cause even of his welfare, of his fulfilment, and indeed of his very continuance — the cause that comes severally to each. For the whole is maimed if you sever anything at all from the connection and continuity, whether of its parts or of its causes; and you sever it, so far as in you lies, whenever you are discontented, and in a manner you destroy it.

title: Meditations
text:
9. Do not feel disgust, nor give up, nor lose heart, if it is not granted you to act in every case from sound principles; but, when struck down, return again, and be glad if the greater part of your acts are worthy of a man, and love that to which you return; and come back to philosophy not as to a schoolmaster, but as the sore-eyed come back to the little sponge and the egg, as another to a plaster, as to a fomentation. For so you will show no parade of obeying reason, but will find rest in it. And remember that philosophy wills only what your own nature wills; but you were willing something else, not according to nature. For what is sweeter than this? Is it not for this that pleasure trips us up? But consider whether magnanimity is not sweeter, and freedom, simplicity, kindness of heart, holiness. For what is sweeter than wisdom itself, when you consider the sureness and the smooth flow, in all things, of the faculty of comprehension and knowledge?
10. Things are wrapped in such a veil, in a manner, that to not a few philosophers, and those no ordinary men, they have seemed altogether incomprehensible; nay, even to the Stoics themselves they seem hard to comprehend; and our every assent is liable to be reversed — for where is the man who never reverses it? Pass on, then, to the objects themselves, how short-lived and cheap they are, and how they may be in the possession of a catamite, a harlot, or a robber. After this, go on to the characters of those who live with you, of whom even the most agreeable can scarcely be borne — not to say that a man can scarcely bear himself. In such darkness and filth, then, and in so great a flux of substance and time, of motion and of things moved, what there is that can be prized or earnestly pursued at all, I cannot conceive. On the contrary, a man should comfort himself by awaiting the natural dissolution, and not chafe at the delay, but find rest in these two thoughts alone: the one, that nothing will befall me which is not in accordance with the Nature of the Whole; the other, that it is in my power to do nothing contrary to my god and guardian spirit; for there is no one who will compel me to transgress against it.
11. To what use, then, am I now putting my soul? On every occasion ask yourself this, and examine: what is now in this part of me which they call the ruling faculty, and whose soul have I now? That of a child? Of a youth? Of a weak woman? Of a tyrant? Of a beast of burden? Of a wild beast?
12. What manner of things those are that pass for good with the many you may gather even from this. For if a man conceived of certain things as truly good — such as wisdom, self-control, justice, courage — then, having first so conceived them, he could not bear to hear the saying "for the abundance of good things," for it would not fit. But of the things that seem good to the many, a man who has first so conceived them will listen, and readily take, as aptly added, the words of the comic poet. So even the many perceive the difference; for otherwise the one saying would not give offence and be rejected, while in the matter of wealth and the good fortunes that minister to luxury or fame we accept it as fittingly and wittily spoken. Go on, then, and ask whether we should honour, and account good, such things, of which, when a man has first conceived them, it could be fittingly added that their possessor, for all his abundance, "has not a place to relieve himself."
13. I am composed of the causal and the material; and neither of these will perish into nothing, just as neither came into being out of nothing. So every part of me will be assigned, by change, to some part of the universe, and that again will change into another part of the universe, and so on to infinity. By such change I too came into being, and those who begot me, and so back to another infinity. For nothing forbids us to speak thus, even if the universe is governed in finite cycles.

title: Meditations
text:
14. Reason and the rational art are powers sufficient to themselves and to their own works. They set out from their own first principle and travel toward the appointed end; and that is why such actions are called "right actions," signifying the rightness of the road.
15. None of those things should be called a man's which do not belong to a man as man. They are not required of a man, nor does the nature of man profess them, nor are they perfections of man's nature. Therefore neither is the end set for man placed in them, nor that which completes the end, the good. For if any of them belonged to a man, it would not have belonged to him to despise them and rise above them; nor would the man who makes himself independent of them be praiseworthy; nor would he who stints himself in any of these be good, if these were goods. But as it is, the more a man strips himself of these or such other things, or bears their being taken from him, by so much the more is he good.
16. Such as are the things you most often picture to yourself, such will your mind be; for the soul is dyed by its impressions. Dye it, then, with a succession of such impressions as these: for instance, that where it is possible to live, there it is also possible to live well; and it is possible to live in a palace; therefore it is also possible to live well in a palace. And again, that each thing is borne toward that for which it was framed; and in that toward which it is borne lies its end; and where its end is, there too lies the advantage and the good of each. Now the good of a rational being is fellowship; for that we are made for fellowship has long since been shown. Or was it not plain that the lower things are for the sake of the higher, and the higher for one another? And living things are higher than the lifeless, and rational beings higher than the rest.
17. To pursue what is impossible is madness; and it is impossible for the base to do otherwise than such things.
18. Nothing befalls any man that he is not framed by nature to bear. The same things befall another, and either through not knowing that they have befallen, or in a display of greatness of soul, he stands firm and remains unhurt. It is a shameful thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.
19. Things themselves touch the soul not at all, nor have they any way into the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul. The soul alone turns and moves itself, and makes the things that present themselves to be such as it deems worthy of itself in its judgments.
20. In one respect man is the nearest thing to us, in so far as we must do men good and bear with them. But in so far as some of them stand in the way of our proper tasks, man becomes for me one of the things indifferent, no less than the sun, the wind, or a wild beast. By these, indeed, some action of mine might be hindered, but they are no hindrance to my impulse and disposition, because of the reservation and the turning about. For the mind turns about and converts every hindrance to its action into something furthering its purpose, and what stands in the way of the work becomes itself the work, and what blocks the road becomes itself the road.
21. Honour that which is most excellent in the universe; and this is that which makes use of all things and directs all things. In like manner honour that which is most excellent in yourself; and this is of the same kind as the other. For in you too it is this that makes use of all else, and by this your life is governed.

title: Meditations
text:
22. What is not harmful to the city does not harm the citizen either. On every impression of being harmed apply this rule: if the city is not harmed by it, neither am I harmed; and if the city is harmed, you must not be angry, but show him who harms the city what he has overlooked.
23. Reflect often on the swiftness with which the things that exist and that come to be are swept by and carried away. For substance is like a river in perpetual flow; the activities are in continual change, and the causes in countless turnings; and there is scarcely anything that stands still, even what is close at hand. And consider, too, the boundless gulf of the past and of the future, in which all things vanish. Is he not, then, a fool who in the midst of all this is puffed up, or distracted, or aggrieved, as though anything could trouble him for any length of time?
24. Remember the whole of substance, of which you partake a very little; and the whole of time, of which a brief and momentary span has been marked off for you; and destiny, of which how small a part are you?
25. Does another do wrong against me? He shall see to it; he has his own disposition, his own activity. I have now what the common nature wills me now to have, and I do what my own nature wills me now to do.
26. Let the ruling and sovereign part of your soul be unmoved by the motions, smooth or rough, in the flesh, and let it not mingle with them, but mark itself off and confine those affections to the parts. But when they are diffused into the mind by that other sympathy, as in a body that is one, then one must not try to resist the sensation, which is natural; only let the ruling faculty not add of itself the opinion that it is good or evil.
27. "To live with the gods." And he lives with the gods who continually shows them his soul content with what is allotted, and doing all that the guardian spirit wills — that spirit which Zeus has given to each man as his guardian and guide, a fragment of himself. And this is each man's mind and reason.
28. Are you angry with the man who reeks like a goat, angry with the man whose breath is foul? What will it profit you? He has such a mouth, such armpits; from such things such an exhalation must needs come. "But the man has reason," you say, "and can, if he reflects, perceive wherein he offends." Good luck to you; then you too have reason. Move his rational disposition by your own rational disposition; show him, remind him. For if he hearkens, you will cure him, and there is no need of anger. Neither tragic actor nor harlot.
29. As you intend to live when you have departed, so it is in your power to live here; but if they do not allow it, then depart from life as well, yet so as to suffer no evil. The room is smoky, and I take my leave; why do you think it a great matter? But while no such thing drives me out, I remain free, and no one will hinder me from doing what I will; and I will what is according to the nature of a rational and social being.
30. The mind of the whole is made for fellowship. At any rate, it has made the lower things for the sake of the higher, and fitted the higher to one another. You see how it has subordinated, co-ordinated, and given to each its due, and brought the most excellent things into concord with one another.
31. How have you borne yourself until now toward gods, parents, brothers, wife, children, teachers, those who reared you, friends, kinsmen, servants? Is it true of you, toward all of them until now, that you have never done an outrage to any nor said an evil word? Recall, too, through what you have passed, and what you have found strength to endure; and that the story of your life is now full, and your service complete; and how many fair things you have seen, and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down upon, how many things accounted glorious you have disregarded, and toward how many thankless men you have been kind.

title: Meditations
text:
32. Why do unskilled and ignorant souls confound the skilled and the knowing? And what soul is skilled and knowing? That which knows the beginning and the end, and the reason which pervades all substance and orders the whole through all eternity in appointed cycles.
33. In a little while you will be ashes or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; and the name is a sound and an echo. And the things highly prized in life are empty, rotten, and trifling — little dogs snapping at one another, quarrelsome children, laughing and then straightway weeping. But good faith, and modesty, and justice, and truth have fled "to Olympus from the wide-wayed earth."
