What, then, still keeps you here, if the objects of sense are ever-changing and unstable, the organs of sense dim and easily misled, the poor soul itself a vapour from the blood, and good repute among such men an empty thing? What then? You will await, serene, whether it be extinction or removal; and until that hour comes, what suffices? What else than to revere and bless the gods, and to do good to men, to bear with them and to forbear; and to remember, of all that lies within the bounds of this poor flesh and breath, that it is neither yours nor in your power?
34. You can always have a smooth course of life, if you can also keep to the right road — if you can comprehend and act by way of method. These two things are common to the soul of God, and of man, and of every rational being: not to be hindered by another, and to find good in a just disposition and conduct, and there to let desire come to rest.
35. If this is neither a vice of mine, nor an action proceeding from a vice of mine, nor is the common good harmed, why do I trouble myself about it? And what harm is there to the common good?
36. Do not be carried away wholesale by the impression. Give help according to your power and as each deserves, even if men are losers in things indifferent; yet do not picture this as a harm; for that is a bad habit. But, as the old man on his departure asked back the foster-child's toy, remembering that it was a toy, so act here too. For indeed, when you take your stand at the rostra — man, have you forgotten what these things were? "Yes; but men are mightily in earnest about them." And will you for that reason be a fool too? I was once, wherever I was overtaken, a man blessed in his lot; but to be blessed in one's lot is to have apportioned to oneself a good lot; and good lots are good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions.
1. The substance of the Whole is docile and pliant; and the reason that governs it has in itself no cause to do evil, for it has no malice, nor does it do anything ill, nor is anything harmed by it. By it all things come to be and are brought to their end.
2. Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting while cold or while warm, drowsy or with sleep enough, ill spoken of or praised, dying or busy with some other thing; for this too, by which we die, is one of the acts of life; and so it is enough, in this too, to make good use of the present.
3. Look within. Let neither the peculiar quality nor the worth of anything escape you.
4. All the things that lie before us will very soon change: either they will be exhaled into vapour, if substance is one, or they will be scattered abroad.
5. The governing reason knows how it is disposed, and what it does, and upon what material.
6. The best way to avenge yourself is not to become like the wrongdoer.

title: Meditations
text:
7. Delight in one thing and rest in it: to pass from one act done for the common good to another act done for the common good, with the remembrance of God.
8. The ruling faculty is that which rouses and turns itself, and makes itself such as it wills, and makes everything that befalls appear to itself such as it wills.
9. According to the Nature of the Whole each thing is brought to pass; for not according to any other nature, whether one that encloses from without, or is enclosed within, or hangs detached outside.
10. Either a medley, a tangle, and a scattering, or a unity, an order, and a providence. If, then, the former, why should I even wish to dwell in such a chance jumble and confusion? Why should I care for anything but how at last I am to "become earth"? Why should I be troubled? For the scattering will come upon me whatever I do. But if the latter is true, then I revere, I stand firm, and I take courage in him who governs.
11. Whenever you are forced, as it were, to be disturbed by your surroundings, return swiftly into yourself, and do not lose the rhythm more than you must; for you will be the more master of the harmony by continually returning to it.
12. If you had at once a stepmother and a mother, you would pay your duty to the one, and yet your return to your mother would be constant. So now the court is your stepmother, and philosophy your mother. Return often to her, and rest in her, by whose help the things at court seem bearable to you, and you bearable in them.
13. As when one forms an impression of meats and such-like foods, that this is the corpse of a fish, that the corpse of a bird or a pig; and again, that Falernian wine is the mere juice of a cluster of grapes, and the purple-bordered robe sheep's hair dipped in the blood of a shellfish; and of the act of generation, that it is the rubbing together of entrails and, with a kind of spasm, the discharge of mucus — such impressions as these, that reach the very things themselves and pass through them, so that one sees what they really are: thus must you do through the whole of life, and where things present themselves as too worthy of trust, lay them bare, behold their cheapness, and strip away the story on which they pride themselves. For vanity is a terrible sophist, and when you think yourself most engaged on serious matters, then most of all are you bewitched. See, at all events, what Crates says of Xenocrates himself.
14. Most of the things the multitude admire come under the most general heads — those things held together by mere cohesion or by nature: stones, wood, fig-trees, vines, olives. Those that men a little more moderate admire come under things held together by a soul: flocks, herds. The things admired by men still more refined come under what is held together by a rational soul — not, however, the universal one, but in so far as it is skilled in some art, or otherwise clever, or merely owns a multitude of slaves. But he who honours the rational, universal, and social soul gives no further heed to the rest, and above all keeps his own soul rational and social in its disposition and its motions, and works together with his kind toward this end.
15. Some things hasten to come into being, others hasten to have been; and of that which is coming to be, some part is already quenched. Flowings and changes continually renew the universe, just as the unceasing course of time makes the infinite age forever new. In this river, then, what among the things rushing past could a man prize, on which there is no standing still? It is as if one began to love one of the little sparrows flitting by, when already it is gone out of sight. Such, indeed, is the very life of each of us, like the exhalation from the blood and the drawing of breath from the air. For just as it is to draw in the air once and give it back, which we do every moment, so it is to give back, there whence you first drew it, the whole power of breathing, which yesterday or the day before you acquired at birth.

title: Meditations
text:
16. It is not the breathing-out, as in plants, that is precious, nor the breathing of cattle and wild beasts, nor the being stamped by impressions, nor the being jerked by impulse like a puppet, nor the herding together, nor the taking of food — for this is like the discharging of the refuse of food. What, then, is precious? To be applauded? No. Then neither to be applauded by tongues; for the praises of the many are an applause of tongues. So you have given up that little fame too. What is left that is precious? This, I think: to be moved and held in check according to one's own constitution, the end to which both occupations and arts lead. For every art aims at this, that the thing it fashions be fitted for the work for which it was fashioned; this the planter and the keeper of the vine seek, this the horse-breaker and the keeper of the dog. And the training of children, and the teaching of them — to what do they hasten? Here, then, is the precious thing; and if this is well with you, you will not procure for yourself any of the rest. Will you not cease to honour many other things besides? Then you will be neither free, nor self-sufficient, nor free from passion; for you must needs envy, be jealous, suspect those able to take such things away, and plot against those who have what you prize. In short, he who lacks any of these things must be in confusion, and moreover often find fault with the gods. But reverence and honour for your own mind will make you pleasing to yourself, well attuned to your fellows, and in harmony with the gods — that is, praising all that they apportion and ordain.
17. Up, down, and round in a circle move the elements; but the motion of virtue is in none of these: it is something more divine, and, advancing by a way hard to trace, it journeys well.
18. What a thing they do! They are unwilling to praise the men who live in the same age and in their own company, yet they set great store by being praised themselves by men who come after, whom they have never seen and never will. This is near to grieving that men of former times did not utter words of praise about you.
19. Do not, if a thing is hard for you to accomplish, suppose it therefore impossible for man; but if anything is possible for man and proper to him, count it attainable by you as well.
20. In the wrestling-ground someone has scratched us with his nails, or, dashing his head against us, has dealt us a blow; yet we do not brand him, nor take offence, nor suspect him thereafter as a plotter. We do, indeed, keep clear of him, yet not as an enemy, nor with suspicion, but with a good-natured avoidance. Let it be so in the other parts of life too: let us overlook many things in those who are, as it were, our fellow-wrestlers. For it is possible, as I said, to avoid them, and neither to suspect nor to hate.
21. If anyone can prove to me, and bring it home, that I think or act wrongly, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth, by which no one was ever harmed. But he is harmed who persists in his own deceit and ignorance.
22. I do my own duty; the other things do not distract me; for they are either lifeless, or irrational, or have lost their way and are ignorant of the road.
23. With irrational creatures and with things and objects in general, deal generously and freely, as one having reason with things that have none; but with men, as having reason, deal in the spirit of fellowship. And in everything call upon the gods. And do not concern yourself how long you will do these things; three hours of such living are enough.

title: Meditations
text:
24. Alexander of Macedon and his muleteer, when they died, came to the same state; for either they were taken back into the same generative principles of the universe, or they were alike scattered into the atoms.
25. Consider how many things, in the same instant of time, happen at once in each of us, both of the body and of the soul; and so you will not wonder if far more things — nay, all the things that come to pass — subsist together in that one and all-embracing whole which we call the universe.
26. If someone puts to you how the name "Antoninus" is written, will you, with straining, force out each of the letters? What, then, if they grow angry — will you grow angry in return? Will you not go on quietly and number off each of the letters? So here too remember that every duty is made up of certain numbered parts. These you must observe, and, without being disturbed or showing ill humour in return to those who show it, carry through methodically the task before you.
27. How cruel it is not to allow men to strive after what appears to them their own and to their advantage. And yet in a way you do not allow them to do this when you are vexed that they go wrong; for they are surely borne along as toward their own and their advantage. "But it is not so." Then teach them, and show them, without being vexed.
28. Death is a rest from the resistance of the senses, from the jerking of impulse like a puppet, from the wandering of thought, and from service to the flesh.
29. It is shameful that, in a life where the body does not give out, the soul should give out first.
30. See that you are not made a Caesar, that you are not dyed with that dye; for it happens. Keep yourself, then, simple, good, sincere, dignified, unaffected, a friend of justice, reverent of the gods, kindly, full of affection, strong for the works that are fitting. Strive to remain such as philosophy wished to make you. Reverence the gods, preserve men. Life is short; the one fruit of earthly life is a holy disposition and acts done for the common good. In all things a disciple of Antoninus: his vigour in all that was done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his holiness, the serenity of his countenance, his sweetness, his contempt of empty fame, his earnestness to grasp the truth of things; how he would never let anything pass without first looking well into it and clearly understanding it; how he bore with those who blamed him unjustly, without blaming them in return; how he hastened at nothing; how he gave no ear to slander; how exact an examiner he was of characters and actions, yet no reviler, not easily startled, not suspicious, no sophist; how content he was with little, in lodging, bed, dress, food, attendance; how laborious and long-suffering; how able to stay at the same task till evening, his frugal diet not even requiring him to relieve himself before the usual hour; the constancy and sameness of his friendships; how he bore with those who freely opposed his opinions, and was glad if anyone showed him something better; and how he was reverent of the gods without superstition. Strive thus, that the last hour may find you with as good a conscience as it found him.
31. Become sober again, and call yourself back; and when you have shaken off sleep and perceived that they were dreams that troubled you, look once more, awake now, on these things as you looked on those.
32. I am composed of a poor body and a soul. To the body all things are indifferent, for it cannot make distinctions. To the mind those things are indifferent that are not its own activities; and all that are its own activities are in its power. Yet even of these it concerns itself only with the present; for its future and past activities are themselves indifferent now.

title: Meditations
text:
33. Pain is no thing contrary to nature for the hand or the foot, so long as the foot does the work of a foot and the hand the work of a hand. So neither is pain contrary to nature for a man, as man, so long as he does the work of a man. And if it is not contrary to nature for him, neither is it an evil to him.
34. What great pleasures robbers, perverts, parricides, and tyrants have enjoyed!
35. Do you not see how the handicraftsmen accommodate themselves up to a point to the layman, yet none the less hold fast to the principle of their craft and cannot bear to depart from it? Is it not strange, then, that the builder and the physician should reverence the principle of their own art more than a man reverences his own — that reason which he shares with the gods?
36. Asia, Europe, are corners of the universe; every sea, a drop of the universe; Athos, a little clod of the universe; all the present, a point in eternity. Everything is small, ever-changing, vanishing away. All things come from there, having set out from that common ruling power, either directly or by consequence. And so the gaping jaws of the lion, and the poison, and every evil-doing — like a thorn, like mire — are by-products of those venerable and beautiful things. Do not, then, imagine them alien to that which you revere, but reflect upon the source of all things.
37. He who has seen the present has seen all things, both all that came to be from everlasting and all that shall be to infinity; for all things are of one kind and one form.
38. Reflect often on the connection of all things in the universe, and their relation to one another. For in a manner all things are interwoven with one another, and so all are dear to one another; for one thing follows in order upon another, by reason of the tension of movement, the common breath, and the unity of substance.
39. Fit yourself to the things with which your lot has been cast; and the men among whom your lot has fallen, love them, but truly.
40. Every instrument, tool, and vessel is in good case if it does the thing for which it was made; and there the maker is not present. But in the things held together by nature, the power that made them is within and abides; wherefore you must the more reverence it, and believe that, if you live and conduct yourself according to its will, you have all things to your mind. So too the Whole has its own things to its mind.
41. Whatever among the things not subject to your choice you have set up for yourself as good or evil, of necessity, on the befalling of such an evil or the failing of such a good, you will blame the gods and hate the men who are the cause, or are suspected of being about to be the cause, of the failing or the befalling; and indeed we do much wrong through our concern for these things. But if we judge those things alone to be good and evil that are in our own power, there remains no cause either to charge against God or to stand toward a man in the posture of an enemy.
42. We all work together toward one accomplishment, some knowingly and with understanding, others without knowing it — just as Heraclitus, I think, says that even those who sleep are workers and fellow-labourers in what comes to pass in the universe. One man works together in one way, another in another; and beyond measure even the man who finds fault and tries to oppose and undo what comes to pass; for the universe had need even of such a one. It remains, then, to understand among which you rank yourself; for he who governs the whole will in any case make good use of you, and receive you as one part of the labourers and fellow-workers. But do not be such a part as the mean and ridiculous verse in the play, of which Chrysippus makes mention.

title: Meditations
text:
43. Does the sun claim to do the work of the rain? Or Asclepius the work of the Fruit-bearer? And what of each of the stars? Are they not different, yet working together toward the same end?
44. If, then, the gods took counsel about me and about what should befall me, they took good counsel; for it is not easy even to conceive of a god without counsel, and for what cause should they be moved to do me harm? What advantage would come of this to them, or to the common good, of which above all they take forethought? But if they took no counsel about me in particular, yet about the common good they certainly took counsel; and the things that befall me by consequence of that I ought to welcome and to love. But if, after all, they take counsel about nothing — which it is not holy to believe; and if not, let us neither sacrifice, nor pray, nor swear by them, nor do the other things we do at every turn as toward gods present and living among us — but if, after all, they take counsel about none of our concerns, then it is in my power to take counsel about myself, and my inquiry is into what is advantageous. And that is advantageous to each which accords with his own constitution and nature; and my nature is rational and social. My city and country, as Antoninus, is Rome; as a man, it is the universe. The things, then, that are of benefit to these cities are alone good for me.
45. Whatever befalls each man is of benefit to the Whole; that would suffice. But further you will observe, as a general rule, if you watch closely, that whatever benefits one man benefits other men too. But here let "benefit" be taken in the more common sense, as applied to things indifferent.
46. As the shows in the amphitheatre and such places weary you, being always the same to behold, and the sameness makes the spectacle cloying, so it is with the whole of life; for all things, up and down, are the same and from the same. How long, then?
47. Reflect continually on all kinds of men, of all kinds of pursuits and of every sort of nation, who have died — so that you come down even to Philistion, Phoebus, and Origanion. Pass now to the other tribes. Thither we too must change our place — where so many mighty orators, so many grave philosophers, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates; so many heroes of old, and so many later generals and tyrants; and besides these Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, and other keen, high-minded, laborious, cunning, and self-willed natures, mockers of the very mortal and fleeting life of men, such as Menippus and the like. Of all these reflect that they have long been laid low. What harm, then, is this to them? And what to those not even named at all? One thing here is worth much: to pass one's life in truth and justice, kindly toward the liars and the unjust.
48. When you wish to gladden yourself, think on the good qualities of those who live with you: in one the energy, in another the modesty, in another the openness of hand, in another something else. For nothing so gladdens as the likenesses of the virtues shining forth in the characters of those who live with us, and meeting together, so far as may be. Therefore one must keep them ready to hand.
49. Are you discontented that you weigh so many pounds and not three hundred? So too be content that you must live so many years and no more; for as you are content with the measure of substance allotted to you, so be content also in the matter of time.
50. Try to persuade them; but act even against their will, when the principle of justice so leads. If, however, anyone resists you with force, betake yourself to contentment and freedom from distress, and use the hindrance for the exercise of another virtue; and remember that you set out with a reservation, and were not aiming at the impossible. At what, then? At an impulse of a certain kind. And this you attain; the things for the sake of which we were set in motion do come to pass.

title: Meditations
text:
51. The lover of fame supposes another's activity to be his own good; the lover of pleasure, his own sensation; but the man of understanding, his own action.
52. It is in your power to hold no opinion about a thing, and so not to be troubled in your soul; for things themselves have no natural power to form our judgments.
53. Accustom yourself to attend closely to what another says, and as far as possible enter into the soul of the speaker.
54. What is not of benefit to the swarm is not of benefit to the bee either.
55. If the sailors spoke ill of the helmsman, or the sick of the physician, would they give heed to anyone else than how he might bring about the safety of the crew or the health of those under his care?
56. How many, with whom I came into the world, have already departed from it!
57. To the jaundiced honey seems bitter, and to one bitten by a mad dog water is a thing of terror, and to children the little ball is fine. Why, then, am I angry? Do you think a false opinion has less force than the bile in the jaundiced or the venom in the man bitten by a mad dog?
58. No one will hinder you from living according to the reason of your own nature; and nothing will befall you contrary to the reason of the common nature.
59. What manner of men are those whom they wish to please, and for what ends, and by what kind of actions! How swiftly will eternity cover all things, and how many it has covered already!
1. What is vice? It is what you have often seen. And on every occasion that befalls, keep ready this thought: this is what you have often seen. Everywhere, up and down, you will find the same things, of which the histories are full — the ancient, the middle, the recent; and of which the cities and the households are full today. There is nothing new; all is familiar and short-lived.
2. How else can your principles be deadened, except by the quenching of the impressions that answer to them — impressions which it is in your power continually to rekindle? I can hold the right opinion about this matter; and if I can, why am I troubled? The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind. Learn this, and you stand upright. You may come back to life; look once more on things as you used to see them; for in this lies the coming back to life.
3. The empty pomp of a procession, plays upon a stage, flocks, herds, sham battles with the spear, a bone thrown to little dogs, a crumb into the fish-ponds, the toils and burden-bearings of ants, the scurrying of frightened mice, puppets pulled by strings. Amid these, then, one must stand kindly and without disdain, yet attending closely to the fact that each man is worth just so much as the things are worth about which he busies himself.
4. One must attend closely, word by word, to what is said, and in every impulse to what is done; and in the latter case see at once toward what end the reference is made, and in the former observe what is the thing meant.
5. Is my understanding equal to this matter or not? If it is equal, I use it for the work as an instrument given me by the Nature of the Whole. If it is not equal, then either I give up the work to one who can accomplish it better, unless for some reason it is my duty not to; or I do it as I can, taking to my aid one who, by the help of my ruling faculty, can do what is now timely and useful for the common good. For whatever I do, by myself or with another, must be directed to this one thing alone: what is useful to the common good and well-fitted to it.

title: Meditations
text:
6. How many who were once much sung have already been given over to oblivion; and how many who sang their praises are long since gone.
7. Be not ashamed to be helped; for the task before you is to do your duty, like a soldier in the storming of a wall. What then, if, being lame, you cannot mount the battlement by yourself, but with another's help it can be done?
8. Let not the future trouble you; for you will come to it, if you must, bearing the same reason that you now use for the present.
9. All things are interwoven with one another, and the bond is holy; and there is hardly anything alien one to another. For all have been ranged together, and together they make up one ordered universe. For there is one universe out of all, and one God pervading all, and one substance, and one law, one reason common to all intelligent beings, and one truth — if indeed there is also one perfection of beings that are of one kind and partake of the same reason.
10. Everything material vanishes very swiftly into the substance of the Whole; every cause is very swiftly taken up into the reason of the Whole; and the memory of everything is very swiftly buried in eternity.
11. To the rational being the same act is at once according to nature and according to reason.
12. Upright, not held upright.
13. As the members of the body are in a unity, such is the relation of rational beings, though separate, who have been framed for one common work. And the thought of this will come home to you the more if you often say to yourself: I am a member of the system made up of rational beings. But if you say you are a part — by changing one letter — you do not yet love men from the heart; doing them good does not yet gladden you as an end in itself; you still do it as a mere propriety, not yet as one doing good to himself.
14. Let what will from without befall the things that can suffer by such befalling. For those things, if they will, may complain of what has befallen them; but I, if I do not suppose that what has befallen is an evil, am not yet harmed. And it is in my power not to suppose it.
15. Whatever anyone may do or say, I must be good; just as if gold, or an emerald, or purple were forever saying, "Whatever anyone may do or say, I must be an emerald and keep my own colour."
16. The ruling faculty does not disturb itself; I mean, it does not frighten itself into desire. If another can frighten it or grieve it, let him do so; for of itself, by its own opinions, it will not turn into such turnings. Let the poor body, if it can, take care that it suffer nothing, and let it say so, if it suffers anything. But the poor soul — that which fears, that which grieves, that which forms any opinion at all about these things — will suffer nothing; for you will not lead it to such a judgment. The ruling faculty, so far as in itself lies, has no needs, unless it make a need for itself; and in the same way it is untroubled and unhindered, unless it trouble and hinder itself.
17. Happiness is a good guardian spirit, a good ruling faculty. What, then, are you doing here, O impression? Be off, by the gods, as you came; for I have no need of you. You have come according to your old custom. I am not angry with you; only go away.
18. Does a man fear change? Why, what can come to be without change? And what is dearer or more familiar to the Nature of the Whole? Can you yourself take a hot bath unless the wood undergoes change? Can you be nourished unless your food undergoes change? Can anything else useful be accomplished without change? Do you not see, then, that for you yourself to undergo change is just the same, and just as necessary to the Nature of the Whole?

title: Meditations
text:
19. Through the substance of the Whole, as through a winter torrent, all bodies pass; bound up with the Whole and working with it, as our limbs work with one another. How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has eternity already swallowed down! And let the same thought come home to you concerning every man whatever and every thing.
20. One thing alone troubles me: that I may not do something which the constitution of man does not will, or as it does not will, or which it does not will now.
21. Near is your forgetting of all things, and near the forgetting of you by all things.
22. It is proper to a man to love even those who stumble. And this comes to pass if it occurs to you at the same time that they are kinsmen, and that they do wrong through ignorance and against their will, and that within a little while both you and they will be dead; and, above all, that the man has done you no harm, for he has not made your ruling faculty worse than it was before.
23. The Nature of the Whole, out of the whole of substance as out of wax, now moulds a little horse; then, melting this down, uses its material for a little tree; then for a little man; then for something else. And each of these has subsisted for a very little while. It is no terrible thing for the box to be broken up, just as its being joined together was no good.
24. A scowling look is greatly against nature; and when it is often assumed, all comeliness dies away, or is at last so quenched that it cannot be rekindled at all. Try, by this very thing, to perceive that it is contrary to reason. For if even the consciousness of doing wrong departs, what reason is left for living?
25. All the things you see the Nature that governs the Whole will very soon change, and out of their substance make other things, and again others out of the substance of those, so that the universe may be ever new.
26. When someone does wrong against you, consider at once with what notion of good or evil he did the wrong. For when you see this, you will pity him, and neither wonder nor be angry. For either you yourself still hold the same thing to be good as he does, or something of the same kind; and then you must forgive him. But if you no longer suppose such things to be good and evil, you will the more easily be kindly toward one who sees amiss.
27. Do not think of what is absent as though it were already present, but of what you have pick out the most fortunate, and on their account remind yourself how they would be longed for if they were not present. Yet at the same time take care lest, by thus rejoicing in them, you accustom yourself to prize them so highly that, should they ever be absent, you will be disturbed.
28. Gather yourself into yourself. It is the nature of the rational ruling faculty to be content with itself when it acts justly, and thereby to keep its calm.
29. Blot out the impression. Stop the jerking of the strings. Mark off the present moment of time. Recognize what is happening, to you or to another. Divide and distinguish the object before you into the causal and the material. Reflect on your last hour. The wrong that another has done — leave it there where the wrong arose.
30. Stretch your thought along with what is said. Let your mind enter into the things that come to pass and the things that act.
31. Make yourself bright with simplicity, modesty, and indifference to all that lies between virtue and vice. Love the human race. Follow God. The poet says that "all things are by convention, and in reality only the elements"; but it is enough to remember that all things are by convention — and these already are very few.

title: Meditations
text:
32. Concerning death: either a scattering, if there are atoms; or, if there is a unity, then extinction or a change of place.
33. Concerning pain: what is unbearable carries us off, and what lasts is bearable. And the mind keeps its own calm by withdrawing into itself, and the ruling faculty is none the worse. But let the parts that are hurt by the pain declare themselves about it, if they can.
34. Concerning fame: look at the minds of those whose praise you seek — what sort they are, and what they shun and what they pursue. And consider that, as one drift of sand heaped upon another hides the first, so in life the things of former times are very swiftly covered by those that come after.
35. From Plato: "Do you suppose that to a mind possessed of greatness and the contemplation of all time and of all substance, human life can seem any great thing?" "It is impossible," said he. "Then such a man will not think death a thing to dread?" "By no means."
36. From Antisthenes: "It is a kingly thing to do well and to be ill spoken of."
37. It is shameful that, while the face is obedient and shapes and orders itself as the mind commands, the mind should not shape and order itself by itself.
38. "Against things, indeed, there is no need to feel anger; for they care nothing for it."
39. "May you grant joy to the immortal gods and to us."
40. "Life is reaped like a ripe ear of corn; and one man is, another is not."
41. "If I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, even this has its reason."
42. "For the right and the good are with me."
43. No joining in lamentation, no fluttering of the heart.
44. From Plato: "But to him I would make this just reply: You speak ill, my friend, if you think that a man worth anything at all should weigh the risk of living or dying, and not rather look to this one thing alone, whenever he acts: whether what he does is just or unjust, the work of a good man or a bad."
45. "For so it stands in truth, men of Athens: wherever a man has stationed himself, thinking it best, or has been stationed by his commander, there he must, as it seems to me, remain and face the danger, taking no account of death or of anything else before the shameful."
46. "But, my good man, see whether nobility and goodness are not something other than saving and being saved. For surely the man who is truly a man must not cling to living for whatever length of time, nor be a lover of his life, but must leave these things to God, and believe the women when they say that no one can escape his destiny, and then consider, on this footing, in what way he may best live the time he has to live."
47. To survey the courses of the stars as one running their course with them, and to reflect continually on the changes of the elements into one another; for the imaginings of these things cleanse away the filth of the life on the ground.
48. A noble saying of Plato's. He who would discourse of men should also look upon earthly things as from some height above: herds, armies, husbandry, marriages, divorces, births, deaths, the uproar of law-courts, desert places, the manifold tribes of barbarians, festivals, lamentations, market-places — all the medley, and the order made out of contraries.
49. Survey the things of the past, the so many changes of dominions. It is possible also to foresee the things that shall be; for they will be wholly of one kind, and it is not possible to step outside the rhythm of the things now coming to pass. Therefore it is all one whether you survey human life for forty years or for ten thousand; for what more will you see?

title: Meditations
text:
50. "And the things that grew from earth go back to earth; but the things that sprang from heavenly seed return again to the vault of heaven." Or else this is a breaking-up of the interlacings of the atoms, and some such scattering of the impassive elements.
51. "With meats and drinks and magic spells turning aside the channel, that they may not die." . . . . . . . . . . . . . "But the gale that blows from God we must endure, and toil on without lamenting."
52. A man may be a better wrestler, but not therefore more fitted for fellowship, nor more modest, nor better ordered in the face of what befalls, nor kindlier toward the failings of his neighbours.
53. Where a work can be accomplished according to the reason common to gods and men, there is nothing to dread; for where it is possible to gain benefit through an activity that prospers and advances in keeping with our constitution, there no harm need be suspected.
54. Everywhere and continually it is in your power to be reverently content with your present lot, to deal justly with the men about you, and to work with art upon your present impression, so that nothing uncomprehended may slip in.
55. Do not look round at the ruling faculties of others, but look straight ahead at this: to what nature is leading you — both the Nature of the Whole, through what befalls you, and your own nature, through what you have to do. And each must do what follows from his constitution; and the other creatures are constituted for the sake of the rational, as everywhere else the lower for the sake of the higher, but rational beings for one another's sake. Now the leading principle in the constitution of man is the social; the second is to be unyielding to the affections of the body; for it is proper to the rational and intelligent motion to mark itself off and never to be overcome by the motion of the senses or of impulse — for both these are animal — but the intelligent motion claims to be first and not to be mastered by them. And justly so; for it is by nature made to use them all. The third thing in the rational constitution is freedom from rashness and from being deceived. Let the ruling faculty, then, holding fast to these, drive straight ahead, and it has what is its own.
56. As one already dead, and having lived only up to the present, you must live the rest of your life, from the surplus, according to nature.
57. Love only that which befalls you and is woven with your destiny; for what could be more fitting?
58. On each thing that befalls, keep before your eyes those to whom the same things happened, and who then were grieved, taken aback, and full of complaint. Where are they now? Nowhere. What then? Will you choose to be like them? Will you not rather leave the alien turnings to those who turn and are turned, and become wholly given over to the question of how to use them? For you will use them well, and they will be material for you; only attend, and will to be good to yourself in everything you do; and remember both these things together: that the act matters, and the matter on which it is done is indifferent.
59. Dig within. Within is the spring of good, and it can always be welling up, if you always dig.
60. The body too should be steady and not flung about, whether in motion or in posture. For just as the mind shows itself in the face, keeping it composed and seemly, so the like is to be required of the whole body. But all this is to be guarded without affectation.
61. The art of living is more like the wrestler's than the dancer's, in that it stands ready and firm against what comes suddenly and unforeseen.

title: Meditations
text:
62. Continually attend to who they are whose testimony you wish to win, and what ruling faculties they have; for then you will neither blame those who stumble unwillingly nor need their witness, when you look into the springs of their opinions and their impulses.
63. "Every soul," he says, "is robbed of truth against its will." So too of justice, of self-control, of kindness, and of everything of the kind. It is most necessary to remember this continually; for so you will be gentler toward all men.
64. On every pain let this be ready to hand: that it is no shame, and does not make the guiding mind worse; for it does not corrupt it, either in so far as it is rational or in so far as it is social. In most pains, indeed, let the saying of Epicurus come to your aid: that pain is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you remember its limits and do not add to it by opinion. Remember this too: that many things which are really pain, though we do not perceive it, are felt as vexations — such as drowsiness, oppressive heat, and loss of appetite. When, then, you are discontented with any of these, say to yourself that you are giving in to pain.
65. See that you never feel toward the inhuman what the inhuman feel toward men.
66. How do we know that Telauges was not better in disposition than Socrates? For it is not enough that Socrates died a more famous death, disputed more cleverly with the sophists, kept watch more enduringly through the cold night, and, when bidden to bring the man of Salamis, seemed more nobly to refuse, and "swaggered in the streets" — about which one might most of all raise a question, if it were true. But this is what we must consider: what manner of soul Socrates had, and whether he could be content to be just toward men and holy toward the gods, neither chafing at vice in vain, nor making himself the slave of any man's ignorance, nor receiving anything allotted to him out of the Whole as something strange, nor enduring it as unbearable, nor lending his mind to share in the affections of the poor flesh.
67. Nature has not so blended you with the compound as not to allow you to mark yourself off and to keep your own under your own control; for it is very possible to be a divine man and yet be recognized by no one. Remember this always, and this too: that very few things are needed for living a happy life; and do not, because you have given up the hope of being a logician and a natural philosopher, on that account despair of being free, modest, social, and obedient to God.
68. To live out your life unconstrained, in the fullest cheerfulness of soul, though all men cry out against you what they will, though the wild beasts tear in pieces the poor limbs of this lump that has grown about you. For amid all this, what prevents the mind from keeping itself in calm, with a true judgment about the things around it and a readiness to use the things put before it — so that the judgment says to what befalls, "This is what you are in your essence, however by opinion you appear otherwise," and the use says to what comes before it, "You are the thing I was seeking"? For to me the present is always material for rational and social virtue, and, in a word, for the art of a man or a god. For everything that befalls is akin either to God or to man, and is neither new nor hard to handle, but familiar and easy to work upon.
69. This is the perfection of character: to pass each day as though it were your last, neither fluttered nor numbed nor playing a part.

title: Meditations
text:
70. The gods, being immortal, are not vexed that throughout so long an age they must always bear with men so many and so worthless; nay, more, they care for them in every way. But you, who are all but at the point of ceasing, do you give up — and that, when you are yourself one of the worthless?
71. It is laughable not to flee one's own vice, which is possible, yet to flee the vice of others, which is impossible.
72. Whatever the rational and social power finds neither intelligent nor social, it justly judges to be inferior to itself.
73. When you have done a good deed and another has been well served by it, why do you, like the foolish, seek besides these a third thing — to be thought to have done a good deed, or to get a return for it?
74. No one wearies of being benefited; and to benefit is an act in accordance with nature. Do not, then, weary of being benefited in the very act of benefiting others.
75. The Nature of the Whole set out upon the making of the universe. Now either everything that comes to pass comes by consequence, or even the chief things, toward which the ruling power of the universe directs its own impulse, are without reason. Remembering this will make you calmer in many things.
1. This too makes for contempt of empty fame, that it is no longer in your power to have lived the whole of your life, or at least your life from youth, as a philosopher; but it has become plain, to many others and to yourself, that you are far from philosophy. You are tainted, then, so that to win the reputation of a philosopher is no longer easy for you; and the conditions of your life fight against it too. If, therefore, you have truly seen where the matter lies, let go of how you will appear, and be content if you live the rest of your life, however long, as your nature wills. Consider, then, what it wills, and let nothing else distract you; for you have learned by trial that, after wandering through how many things, you nowhere found the good life — not in syllogisms, not in wealth, not in fame, not in enjoyment, nowhere. Where then is it? In doing what man's nature seeks. How, then, will you do these things? If you hold principles from which your impulses and actions flow. What principles? Those concerning good and evil: that nothing is good for a man which does not make him just, self-controlled, brave, free; and nothing evil which does not make him the contrary of these.
2. On every act ask yourself: how is this to me? Shall I not repent of it? In a little while I am dead, and all is past and gone. What more do I seek, if the present work is that of an intelligent being, made for fellowship and under the same law as God?
3. Alexander, Gaius, and Pompey — what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? For these men saw into things, and their causes, and their material, and their ruling faculties were the same; but as for those, how many things had they to provide for, of how many were they the slaves!
4. They will none the less do the same things, even if you burst with rage.
5. First, do not be troubled; for all things are according to the Nature of the Whole, and in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, as neither Hadrian is, nor Augustus. Then, fixing your gaze on the matter, see it as it is, and remembering that you must be a good man, and what the nature of man requires, do that without swerving, and speak as it seems to you most just — only kindly, and modestly, and without pretence.
6. The Nature of the Whole has this work: to transfer the things that are here to there, to change them, to take them up from one place and carry them to another. All is alteration — yet not such that you should fear any new thing: all is familiar, and the apportionments too are equal.

title: Meditations
text:
7. Every nature is content with itself when it goes well; and the rational nature goes well when, in its impressions, it assents to nothing false or obscure; when it directs its impulses only toward acts done for the common good; when it limits its desires and aversions to the things in our power; and when it welcomes all that is allotted by the common nature. For it is a part of that nature, as the nature of the leaf is part of the nature of the plant — except that there the nature of the leaf is part of a nature without sense or reason, and one that can be hindered, while the nature of man is part of a nature that cannot be hindered, that is intelligent and just, since it makes equal and proportionate the apportionments of time, substance, cause, activity, and circumstance to each. But look not whether you find one thing equal to one thing in every case, but whether, taken altogether, the sum of one man's lot is equal to the sum of another's.
8. You cannot read. But you can keep down insolence; you can rise above pleasures and pains; you can be above the love of fame; you can refrain from anger at the senseless and ungrateful, and even care for them.
9. Let no one any longer hear you finding fault with the life at court, nor hear yourself.
10. Repentance is a kind of self-reproach for having let slip something useful; and the useful must be something good, and the good and noble man must take care of it. But no good and noble man would ever repent of having let slip some pleasure; therefore pleasure is neither useful nor good.
11. What is this thing in itself, in its own constitution? What is its substance and material, what its cause, what does it do in the universe, and how long does it subsist?
12. When you rise unwillingly from sleep, remind yourself that it is according to your constitution and according to the nature of man to render acts that serve the fellowship, whereas sleeping is shared even with the irrational creatures. And what is according to nature for each is more proper to it, more akin, and indeed more pleasant.
13. Continually, and on every impression if it can be done, apply natural science, the science of the passions, and logic.
14. Whomever you meet, say to yourself at once: what principles has this man about good and evil? For if he has such-and-such principles about pleasure and pain and the causes of each, about fame and obscurity, death and life, it is no wonder, nor will it seem strange to me, if he does such-and-such things; and I shall remember that he is compelled to act so.
15. Remember that, just as it is shameful to be surprised that the fig-tree bears figs, so it is to be surprised that the universe bears the things of which it is the bearer. And it is shameful for a physician or a helmsman to be surprised if a man has a fever, or if a contrary wind has arisen.
16. Remember that to change your course, and to follow one who sets you right, is no less an act of freedom than to keep to your course; for it is your own activity, accomplished according to your own impulse and judgment, and indeed according to your own mind.
17. If it lies with you, why do you do it? If with another, whom do you blame — the atoms, or the gods? Either is madness. No one is to be blamed. For if you can, set it right; but if you cannot, set the matter itself right; and if you cannot do even this, to what end does blaming bring you? For nothing should be done at random.
18. What dies does not fall outside the universe. If it remains here and changes here, it is also dissolved here into its own parts, which are elements of the universe and of you. And these too change, and do not grumble.

title: Meditations
text:
19. Everything has come into being for some purpose — a horse, a vine. Why do you wonder? Even the Sun will say, "I have come into being for some work," and so the other gods. For what, then, have you? To take pleasure? See whether the thought can bear it.
20. Nature has aimed at each thing in its ending no less than in its beginning and its course, as one who tosses a ball. What good is it, then, to the little ball to be thrown up, or what evil to come down, or even to fall? And what good to the bubble while it holds together, or what evil when it bursts? The like is true also of a lamp.
21. Turn it inside out and see what it is; what it becomes when it grows old, when it falls sick, when it is debauched. Short-lived are both praiser and praised, both he who remembers and he who is remembered. And all this in a corner of this region; and not even here are all in agreement, nor a man even with himself; and the whole earth is a point.
22. Attend to the matter before you, whether it be a principle, an action, or a meaning. You suffer this justly; for you choose to become good tomorrow rather than to be good today.
23. Am I doing something? I do it, referring it to the good of men. Does something befall me? I receive it, referring it to the gods and the source of all things, from which all that comes to pass is woven together.
24. As bathing appears to you — oil, sweat, filth, greasy water, all loathsome — such is every part of life, and everything that lies before us.
25. Lucilla buried Verus, then Lucilla was buried. Secunda buried Maximus, then Secunda. Epitynchanus buried Diotimus, then Epitynchanus. Antoninus buried Faustina, then Antoninus. Such is the way of all things. Celer buried Hadrian, then Celer. And those keen-witted men, the seers, the puffed-up — where are they? Keen-witted men like Charax, Demetrius the Platonist, Eudaemon, and any such. All of a day, dead long since; some not even remembered for a little while; some turned into legends; some already faded even from the legends. Remember, then, that this compound of yours must either be scattered, or its breath be quenched, or it must move elsewhere and be assigned to another place.
26. The joy of a man is to do what is proper to a man; and proper to a man is goodwill toward his kind, contempt of the motions of sense, the discernment of plausible impressions, and the contemplation of the Nature of the Whole and of the things that come to be according to it.
27. There are three relations: one to the vessel that encloses you; one to the divine cause, from which all things befall all; and one to those who live with you.
28. Pain is either an evil to the body — let the body then declare it — or to the soul; but the soul can keep its own clear sky and calm, and not suppose it to be an evil. For every judgment, impulse, desire, and aversion is within, and nothing of evil mounts up here.
29. Blot out your impressions, continually saying to yourself: it is now in my power that there be in this soul no wickedness, no desire, in short no disturbance at all, but that, seeing all things as they are, I use each according to its worth. Remember this power, which is according to nature.
30. Speak both in the Senate and to anyone whatever in seemly fashion, not over-precisely; use sound speech.
31. The court of Augustus — wife, daughter, grandchildren, ancestors, sister, Agrippa, kinsmen, household, friends, Areius, Maecenas, physicians, sacrificers — the death of a whole court. Then pass to the others . . . not the death of a single man, but of houses like that of the Pompeii. And that which is inscribed on the tombs, "the last of his line" — reflect how many before them strove to leave behind a successor, and then it was needful that someone should be the last; here again the death of a whole line.

title: Meditations
text:
32. You must compose your life action by action, and be content if each does its own work as well as may be; and that it should do its own work no one can prevent. "But something from without will stand in the way." Nothing will stand in the way of acting justly, temperately, and reasonably. "But perhaps some other activity will be hindered." Yet by contentment with the very hindrance, and by a good-tempered passing to what is granted, another action is at once set in its place, one that will fit into the composition of which we speak.
33. Receive without arrogance, let go without clinging.
34. If ever you have seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a head severed and lying somewhere apart from the rest of the body, such does a man make himself, so far as in him lies, who is unwilling to accept what befalls and cuts himself off, or who does anything against the fellowship. You have somehow flung yourself out of the natural unity, for you were born a part; but now you have cut yourself off. Yet here is the gracious thing: it is in your power to unite yourself again. To no other part has God granted, once severed and cut off, to come together again; but consider the kindness with which he has honoured man. For he has put it in his power not to be broken off from the whole at all; and, if he is broken off, to return again and to grow together and to take back his place as a part.
35. As the other powers in each rational being come from the nature of rational beings, so does this one too. For as that nature converts and ranges in the order of destiny every obstacle and resistance, and makes it a part of itself, so the rational being too can make every hindrance material for itself, and use it for whatever it set out to do.
36. Do not let the picture of your whole life confound you; do not dwell on all the troublesome things, of what kind and how many, that may probably befall; but on each present occasion ask yourself: what is there in this task unbearable and past endurance? For you will be ashamed to confess it. Then remind yourself that neither the future nor the past weighs upon you, but always the present; and this is made small, if you mark it off by itself, and rebuke your mind if it cannot hold out against this bare present.
37. Does Pantheia or Pergamus now sit beside the bier of Verus? Or Chabrias or Diotimus beside that of Hadrian? Absurd. And if they did sit there, would the dead perceive it? And if they perceived it, would they be pleased? And if they were pleased, would those mourners thereby become immortal? Was it not fated that these too should first become old men and old women, and then die? And what, after these were dead, were the others to do? All this is a stench and corruption in a bag.
38. If you can see sharply, look — and judge, he says, with the wisest of judgments.
39. In the constitution of the rational being I see no virtue set against justice; but against pleasure I see self-control.
40. If you take away your own opinion about that which seems to grieve you, you yourself stand in the safest place. "Who is 'yourself'?" Reason. "But I am not reason." Be it so. Then let reason at least not grieve itself; and if some other part of you is in a bad state, let it form its own opinion about itself.
41. The hindering of perception is an evil to the sentient nature. The hindering of impulse is likewise an evil to the sentient nature. And there is something else likewise that hinders and is an evil to the constitution of plants. So, then, the hindering of mind is an evil to the intelligent nature. Apply all this to yourself. Does pain, does pleasure, lay hold of you? The senses will see to it. Has a hindrance met your impulse? If you set out without reservation, then it is at once an evil to you as a rational being; but if you take the common course, you are not yet harmed nor hindered. As for the things proper to the mind, no one else is wont to hinder them; for neither fire, nor steel, nor a tyrant, nor slander, nor anything whatever lays hold of it, once it has become "a rounded sphere at rest in its roundness."

title: Meditations
text:
42. I am not worthy to grieve myself; for I never willingly grieved another.
43. One thing gladdens one man, another another; but I am gladdened if I keep my ruling faculty sound, turning away from no man and from nothing that befalls men, but looking on all things with kindly eyes, receiving them, and using each according to its worth.
44. See, make this present time a gift to yourself. Those who rather pursue fame hereafter do not reckon that the men who shall come after will be such as those they now find burdensome; and those men too are mortal. And what, in any case, is it to you if they ring out such voices about you, or hold such an opinion of you?
45. Take me up and cast me where you will; for there too I shall keep my guardian spirit serene — that is, content, if it can be and act in keeping with its own constitution. Is this thing worth so much that, for its sake, my soul should be in evil case and worse than itself, abased, craving, fawning, scared? And what will you find worth so much?
46. To no man can anything befall that is not a circumstance proper to man, nor to an ox what is not proper to an ox, nor to a vine what is not proper to a vine, nor to a stone what is not proper to a stone. If, then, there befalls each what is wont and natural to it, why should you be discontented? For the common nature has brought you nothing unbearable.
47. If you are grieved by something external, it is not that thing that troubles you, but your own judgment about it; and this it is in your power to blot out forthwith. But if you are grieved by something in your own disposition, who prevents you from setting your principle right? And likewise, if you are grieved because you are not doing some particular thing that seems sound to you, why not do it rather than grieve? "But something stronger stands in the way." Then do not grieve; for the cause of its not being done does not lie with you. "But life is not worth living if this is not done." Then take your leave of life kindly, even as one who accomplishes his work dies, and at peace with the things that stood in your way.
48. Remember that the ruling faculty becomes invincible when, gathered into itself, it is content with itself, doing nothing it does not will, even if its resistance be unreasonable. What then, when it judges of a thing with reason and after careful consideration? Therefore the mind free from passions is a citadel; for a man has nothing stronger to which he may flee for refuge and be thereafter unassailable. He, then, who has not seen this is unlearned; but he who has seen it and does not flee thither is unfortunate.
49. Say to yourself no more than the first impressions report. It has been reported to you that so-and-so speaks ill of you. This has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that he is in danger I do not see. So, then, always abide by the first impressions, and add nothing to them from within, and nothing befalls you — or rather, add something, as one who knows each of the things that come to pass in the universe.
50. A bitter cucumber? Throw it away. Brambles in the path? Turn aside. That is enough; do not add, "Why were these things made in the universe?" For you will be laughed at by a man versed in nature, just as you would be laughed at by a carpenter or a cobbler if you found fault with them for the shavings and parings of their work that you see in the shop. And yet those men have somewhere to throw such things, while the Nature of the Whole has nothing outside herself; but the wonder of this art is that, having marked off her own bounds, she changes back into herself everything within that seems to be decaying, growing old, and useless, and again makes other new things out of these very things, so that she neither needs substance from without nor has need of anywhere to cast out what is rotted. She is content, then, with her own space, her own material, and her own art.

title: Meditations
text:
51. Neither be slovenly in your actions, nor confused in your talk, nor wandering in your impressions; nor, in your soul, let it be wholly drawn together or flung apart; nor in your life be so taken up with business that there is no leisure. "They kill, they hack to pieces, they pursue with curses." What is that to keeping the mind pure, sane, sober, just? It is as though a man, standing beside a clear and sweet spring, should curse it, while it never ceases to well up with water fit to drink; and though he throw in mud, or dung, it will very quickly disperse and wash them away, and will in no way be stained. How, then, will you possess an ever-flowing spring and not a mere cistern? If you guard yourself, every hour, in freedom, together with kindness, simplicity, and modesty.
52. He who does not know what the universe is does not know where he is. And he who does not know for what he was born does not know who he is, nor what the universe is. And he who has failed in any one of these could not even say for what he himself was born. What manner of man, then, does he seem to you, who flees from or pursues the praise of those who applaud — men who know neither where they are nor who they are?
53. Do you wish to be praised by a man who curses himself three times an hour? Do you wish to please a man who does not please himself? And does he please himself who repents of nearly everything he does?
54. No longer merely breathe in common with the air that surrounds you, but now think also in common with the intelligence that surrounds all things. For the intelligent power is poured out and spread abroad on every side, no less, for him who can draw it in, than the airy power for him who can breathe.
55. Vice, taken generally, does no harm to the universe; and vice in particular does no harm to anyone else, but is harmful only to him to whom it has been granted to be rid of it, the moment he so wills.
56. To my faculty of choice the faculty of choice of my neighbour is as indifferent as his breath and his flesh. For even though we are made above all for one another's sake, still each of our ruling faculties has its own sovereignty; otherwise the vice of my neighbour would be an evil to me, which God did not see fit to allow, lest it should lie in another's power to make me unhappy.
57. The sun seems to be poured down, and on every side indeed it is poured out, yet not poured away. For this pouring is a stretching forth; whence its beams are called rays, from their being stretched out. And what manner of thing a ray is you may see, if you observe the sun's light coming in through a narrow chink into a darkened room; for it is stretched out in a straight line and rests, as it were, against any solid that meets it and bars the air beyond; and there it stays, and does not slip down or fall. Such, then, should be the pouring and spreading of the mind: in no way a pouring away, but a stretching forth; and toward the hindrances it meets it should make no violent or impetuous thrust, nor fall down, but stand and shed light on what receives it. For what does not transmit the ray will of itself rob itself of the light.
58. He who fears death fears either to lose all sensation or to gain a sensation of another kind. But if you will have no sensation, neither will you feel any evil; and if you gain a different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of being, and will not cease to live.
59. Men have come into being for one another's sake. Either instruct them, then, or bear with them.

title: Meditations
text:
60. In one way an arrow is borne, in another the mind. Yet the mind, even when it takes care and turns about in its inquiry, is borne none the less straight forward toward its object.
61. To enter into the ruling faculty of every man, and to grant to every other man also to enter into your own.
1. He who does wrong commits an impiety. For since the Nature of the Whole has framed rational beings for one another's sake, so as to help one another according to desert but in no way to harm, he who transgresses her will plainly commits an impiety against the most venerable of the gods. And the liar too is impious toward the same goddess; for the Nature of the Whole is the nature of the things that are, and the things that are stand in kinship with all that exists. Moreover, she is named Truth, and is the first cause of all that is true. He, then, who lies of his own will is impious, in so far as by deceiving he does wrong; and he who lies against his will, in so far as he is at variance with the Nature of the Whole, and in so far as he brings disorder by fighting against the nature of the universe. For he fights against it who is carried, of himself, toward what is contrary to the truth; for he had received from nature the starting-points, and, having neglected them, he is now unable to distinguish the false from the true. And again, he who pursues pleasures as goods, and flees pains as evils, is impious. For such a man must needs often find fault with the common nature, as apportioning something not according to desert to the bad and the good — since the bad are often in the midst of pleasures and acquire the things that make them, while the good fall in with pain and the things that make it. Further, he who fears pains will one day fear some of the things that must come to pass in the universe, and this is already impious; and he who pursues pleasures will not refrain from doing wrong, and this is plainly impious. But toward those things to which the common nature is indifferent — for she would not have made both, were she not indifferent to both — toward these those too who would follow nature, being of one mind with her, must be indifferent. Whoever, then, is not himself indifferent toward pain and pleasure, death and life, fame and obscurity, which the Nature of the Whole uses indifferently, plainly commits an impiety. And by saying that the common nature uses these indifferently, I mean that they befall indifferently, in due sequence, the things that come to be and follow upon them, by some ancient impulse of providence, according to which, from some beginning, she set out upon this ordering of things, having conceived certain principles of what should be, and marked off generative powers of substances, changes, and successions of this kind.
2. It were the part of a more gracious man to depart from among men having had no taste of falsehood, of all hypocrisy, of luxury, and of pride. But to breathe out one's last when sated with these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to settle down with vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague far worse than any such ill-tempering and alteration of this enveloping air. The one is a plague of living creatures, as living creatures; the other a plague of men, as men.
3. Do not despise death, but be content with it, as one of the things that nature wills. For such as it is to be young and to grow old, to grow up and to come to one's prime, to cut teeth and grow a beard and turn grey, to beget, to conceive, and to bring forth, and all the other natural workings that the seasons of life bring — such is dissolution too. It is, then, the part of a man who has reasoned things out not to be heedless, headstrong, or scornful toward death, but to await it as one of the workings of nature; and as you now await the time when the child shall come forth from your wife's womb, so look for the hour in which your poor soul shall fall out of this husk. But if you wish for a homely rule that touches the heart, nothing will make you so content with death as the marking of those objects from which you are about to be parted, and the characters with which your soul will no longer be entangled. For you must by no means be offended with them, but care for them and bear with them gently; yet remember that your release will not be from men who share your principles. For this alone, if anything, could hold you back and keep you in life, were it permitted to live among those who had acquired the same principles. But as it is, you see how great is the weariness of the discord of living together, so that you may say: "Come quickly, O death, lest perchance I too forget myself."

title: Meditations
text:
4. He who does wrong does wrong to himself; he who does injustice does it to himself, making himself bad.
5. Often he does wrong who does not do something, not only he who does something.
6. It is enough that your present opinion be one that grasps the truth, your present act one for the common good, your present disposition one content with all that befalls from the cause outside.
7. Blot out the impression; check the impulse; quench desire; keep the ruling faculty in your own power.
8. Among the irrational creatures one soul is distributed; among rational beings one intelligent soul is apportioned: just as there is one earth of all that is earthy, and we see by one light, and breathe one air, all of us that have sight and life.
9. All things that share in something common hasten toward what is of their own kind. All that is earthy inclines toward earth; all that is watery flows together; the airy likewise, so that they need barriers and force to keep them apart. Fire rises upward by reason of the elemental fire, but is so ready to be kindled along with every fire here that even all material a little drier is easily kindled, because there is less mingled in it to hinder kindling. And so too everything that partakes of the common intelligent nature hastens likewise, or even more, toward what is akin to it; for the more excellent it is beyond the rest, by so much the readier is it to blend and to mingle with its own kind. At once, then, among the irrational, there were found swarms and herds and the rearing of young and a kind of love; for there were already souls there, and the binding power was found heightened in the more excellent, as it was not in plants, or stones, or wood. And among rational beings there were found commonwealths, friendships, households, assemblies, and, in wars, treaties and truces. And among things still more excellent, a kind of unity subsisted even between things far apart, as among the stars; so that the ascent to the more excellent could work sympathy even in things separated. See, then, what now comes to pass: for the intelligent beings alone have now forgotten their eagerness and inclination toward one another, and here alone the flowing-together is not seen. Yet, flee as they may, they are caught up nonetheless; for nature prevails. You will see what I mean if you watch closely; for one would sooner find some earthy thing touching nothing earthy than a man wholly severed from man.
10. Both man and God and the universe bear fruit; each bears it in its own seasons. If usage has, strictly speaking, worn the word smooth for the vine and the like, that is no matter. Reason too has its fruit, both common and proper, and there come from it other things such as reason itself is.
11. If you can, teach men better; but if not, remember that kindness was given you for this. The gods too are kind to such men, and even work together with them in some things, toward health, toward wealth, toward fame — so good are they. And it is in your power too; or tell me, who is hindering you?
12. Labour, not as one wretched, nor as one wishing to be pitied or admired; but will this one thing only: to be moved and held in check as the reason of the commonwealth requires.
13. Today I escaped from every trouble — or rather, I cast out every trouble; for it was not outside, but within, in my own opinions.
14. All these things are familiar by experience, of a day in their duration, sordid in their matter; all is now as it was in the days of those whom we have buried.

title: Meditations
text:
15. Things stand outside the door, by themselves, knowing nothing of themselves and pronouncing nothing about themselves. What, then, pronounces about them? The ruling faculty.
16. Not in being acted upon, but in acting, lies the good and evil of the rational and social being; just as neither his virtue nor his vice lies in being acted upon, but in acting.
17. To the stone thrown up there is no evil in coming down, nor any good in being thrown up.
18. Pass within, into their ruling faculties, and you will see what judges you fear, and what manner of judges they are even concerning themselves.
19. All things are in change; and you yourself are in continual alteration and, in a way, in decay; and so is the whole universe.
20. Another's fault you must leave there with him.
21. The ending of an activity, the rest of an impulse and an opinion, is, as it were, their death — and no evil. Pass now to the ages of life — childhood, boyhood, youth, old age; for the change of each of these too is a death. Was there anything dreadful in it? Pass now to the life under your grandfather, then to that under your mother, then to that under your father; and finding many other dissolutions, changes, and endings, ask yourself: was there anything dreadful? So, then, neither is the ending and rest and change of your whole life anything dreadful.
22. Hasten to your own ruling faculty, and to that of the Whole, and to this man's. To your own, that you may make it a just mind; to that of the Whole, that you may remember of what you are a part; to this man's, that you may consider whether it is ignorance or design, and at the same time reckon that he is your kinsman.
23. As you yourself are a part that completes a civic system, so let every act of yours be one that completes the civic life. Whatever act of yours, then, has no reference, near or far, to the social end, this tears your life apart and does not let it be one, and is seditious — as in a community the man who, for his own part, stands aloof from such concord.
24. Children's tantrums and playthings, and "little souls bearing corpses," so that the tale of the Descent into the Dead comes home to us more vividly.
25. Go to the quality of the cause, and, marking it off from the material, contemplate it; then mark off also the time, the utmost that this thing of such-and-such a quality is by nature fitted to subsist.
26. You have endured countless troubles through not being content with your ruling faculty doing the things for which it was framed. But enough.
27. When another blames you, or hates you, or men utter such things, go to their poor souls, pass within, and see what manner of men they are. You will see that you need not be anxious that they should hold some opinion or other about you. Yet you must be kindly toward them; for by nature they are friends, and the gods too help them in all manner of ways, through dreams and oracles — and that, too, in the very things about which they are concerned.
28. The cycles of the universe are the same, up and down, from age to age. And either the mind of the Whole sets itself in motion toward each particular thing — and if this is so, accept what it sets in motion; or it set itself in motion once, and the rest follows by consequence — and why should you be anxious about this? For in a manner the universe is either atoms or an indivisible whole. In sum: if it is God, all is well; if it is at random, do not you too be at random. Soon earth will cover us all; then earth too will change, and those things will change to infinity, and again these to infinity. For one who reflects on the wave upon wave of changes and alterations, and on their swiftness, will despise everything mortal.

title: Meditations
text:
29. The substance of the Whole is a winter torrent; it bears all things along. How cheap, then, are these little men who busy themselves with affairs of state and, as they suppose, act like philosophers — full of snot! Man, what then? Do what nature now requires; set about it, if it is granted you, and do not look round to see whether anyone will know. Do not hope for Plato's Republic, but be content if the smallest thing goes forward, and reflect how small a matter even the outcome of that is. For who will change men's principles? And without a change of principles, what is there but the slavery of men who groan and pretend to obey? Go on now, and tell me of Alexander and Philip and Demetrius of Phalerum. They shall see to it, if they saw what the common nature willed, and schooled themselves; but if they played the tragedian, no one has condemned me to imitate them. The work of philosophy is simple and modest; do not lead me away into solemn humbug.
30.
