To survey from above the countless herds, the countless rites, the voyaging of every kind in storms and calms, and the differences among things coming into being, joined together, and passing away. Reflect too on the life lived long ago by others, and the life to be lived after you, and the life lived now among the barbarian nations; and how many do not even know your name, and how many will very soon forget it, and how many who perhaps praise you now will very soon blame you; and how neither memory is a thing worth speaking of, nor fame, nor anything else whatever.
31. Calm, as regards what befalls from the cause outside; and justice, in the things done by the cause that proceeds from you: that is, an impulse and action ending in this very thing, to act for the common good, as being according to your nature.
32. You can strip away many superfluous things that trouble you, things that lie wholly in your opinion; and you will at once make for yourself ample room, by grasping the whole universe in your thought, by reflecting on everlasting time, and by considering the swift change of each particular thing — how brief the span from birth to dissolution, how vast the gulf before birth, and how the time after dissolution is likewise infinite.
33. All that you see will very soon perish, and those who have watched it perish will themselves very soon perish too; and he who dies in extreme old age will be brought to the same state as he who dies before his time.
34. What are the ruling faculties of these men, and about what have they been in earnest, and for what do they love and honour? Think that you see their poor souls naked. When they suppose that they do harm by their blame, or benefit by their praise, how great is their conceit!
35. Loss is nothing other than change. And in this the Nature of the Whole delights, by which all things come to be well, and from everlasting came to be in like kind, and to infinity will be other such things. Why, then, do you say that all things came to be ill, and all things will forever be ill, and that no power, after all, was ever found among so many gods to set these things right, but the universe is condemned to be held fast in unceasing evils?
36. The rottenness of the material that lies beneath each thing: water, dust, little bones, a stench. Or again: marble is but callosities of the earth, and gold and silver its dregs; the robe is hair, and the purple is blood; and all else is of the same kind. And the breath too is another such thing, changing out of these into these.

title: Meditations
text:
37. Enough of this wretched life, and grumbling, and aping! Why are you troubled? What is new in this? What unsettles you? The cause? Look at it. Or the material? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing; but become at last, toward the gods too, simpler and better. It is all one whether you survey these things for a hundred years or for three.
38. If he did wrong, the evil is there, with him. But perhaps he did not do wrong.
39. Either all things flow from one intelligent source and befall as in one body, and the part must not find fault with what is done for the Whole; or there are atoms, and nothing but a medley and a scattering. Why, then, are you troubled? Say to your ruling faculty: are you dead, are you corrupted, are you turned into a beast, do you play a part, do you herd with the rest, do you graze?
40. Either the gods can do nothing, or they can do something. If, then, they can do nothing, why do you pray? But if they can, why not rather pray that they grant you neither to fear any of these things, nor to desire any of them, nor to grieve over any of them, rather than that something be present or absent? For surely, if they can work together with men, they can work together toward these things too. But perhaps you will say: "The gods have put these in my own power." Then is it not better to use what is in your power with freedom, than to busy yourself with what is not in your power, in slavery and abjection? And who told you that the gods do not work together with us even in the things in our power? Begin, at all events, to pray for these things, and you will see. The one prays, "How may I lie with that woman?" Do you pray, "How may I not desire to lie with her?" Another, "How may I be rid of that man?" Do you, "How may I not wish to be rid of him?" Another, "How may I not lose my little child?" Do you, "How may I not fear to lose him?" In short, turn your prayers this way, and see what comes of it.
41. Epicurus says: "In my sickness my conversations were not about the sufferings of my poor body, nor did I talk such things to those who came in, but I went on discussing the chief points of natural philosophy, and was intent on this very thing: how the mind, though sharing in such motions of the poor flesh, may yet remain unperturbed, keeping its own good. Nor did I give the physicians occasion to give themselves airs, as though they were doing something great; but my life went on well and nobly." Do then as he did, in sickness, if you are sick, and in any other circumstance. For not to forsake philosophy in whatever befalls, nor to babble idly with the layman and the man ignorant of nature, is common to every school. Be intent only on what is now being done, and on the instrument by which you do it.
42. When you are offended at someone's shamelessness, ask yourself at once: can it be, then, that shameless men should not exist in the universe? It cannot. Do not, then, demand the impossible; for this man too is one of those shameless ones who must of necessity exist in the universe. Let the same thought be ready to hand concerning the rogue, the faithless, and everyone who does any wrong whatever; for the moment you remember that the race of such men cannot but exist, you will be kindlier toward each of them. And it is useful, too, to consider at once what virtue nature has given man against this very fault; for she has given gentleness as an antidote against the thankless man, and against another some other power. And in any case it is in your power to teach better the man who has gone astray; for everyone who does wrong misses the mark set before him and has gone astray. And besides, how have you been harmed? For you will find that none of those at whom you are exasperated has done anything of a kind to make your mind worse; and it is here that your evil and your harm have their whole existence. And what is new or strange in it, if the uninstructed man does the deeds of the uninstructed? See whether you ought not rather to blame yourself, that you did not expect this man to do this wrong; for you had the means, drawn from reason, to reflect that it was likely he would do this wrong, and yet, forgetting it, you wonder that he has done wrong. But above all, when you find fault with a man as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself; for the fault is plainly your own, whether you trusted that a man of such a disposition would keep faith, or, in granting a favour, did not grant it for its own sake, nor so as to have received your whole reward straightway from the very act. For what more do you want, when you have done a man a good turn? Is it not enough that you have done something according to your nature, but do you seek a reward for it? As though the eye should demand a recompense for seeing, or the feet for walking. For just as these were made for this, and, in working according to their own constitution, have what is their own, so too man, being made by nature to do good, whenever he does something of benefit, or otherwise helpful in things indifferent, has done that for which he was framed, and has what is his own.

title: Meditations
text:
1. Will you ever, my soul, be good and simple and one and naked, more manifest than the body that surrounds you? Will you ever taste of a loving and affectionate disposition? Will you ever be full and in want of nothing, longing for nothing, desiring nothing, neither living thing nor lifeless, for the enjoyment of pleasures? Nor any time in which to enjoy them the longer; nor any place or region or fair climate; nor any harmony of men? But will you be content with your present state, and take pleasure in all that is present, and persuade yourself that all things are present to you from the gods, and that all is well for you and will be well — all that they love, and all that they intend to give for the preservation of that perfect being, the good and just and beautiful, which begets all things and holds them together and embraces them and gathers them in as they are dissolved for the begetting of other like things? Will you ever be such as to dwell together with gods and men in such a way as neither to find any fault with them nor to be condemned by them?
2. Observe what your nature requires, in so far as you are governed by mere nature; then do it and accept it, if your nature as a living being is not going to be made worse by it. Next, you must observe what your nature as a living being requires, and accept all this, if your nature as a rational living being is not going to be made worse by it. And the rational is at once the social. Using these rules, then, busy yourself with nothing further.
3. Everything that befalls befalls either in such a way that you are by nature fitted to bear it, or in such a way that you are not. If, then, what befalls you is such as you are fitted to bear, do not be discontented, but bear it as you are fitted to. But if it is such as you are not fitted to bear, do not be discontented; for it will destroy you and so be itself destroyed. Yet remember that you are by nature fitted to bear everything which it lies in your own opinion to make bearable and endurable, by an impression of its being your advantage, or your duty, to do this.
4. If he goes wrong, instruct him kindly, and show him what he has overlooked. But if you cannot, blame yourself — or not even yourself.
5. Whatever befalls you was prepared for you from everlasting, and the interweaving of causes wove together both your own existence from all eternity and the coming-to-pass of this thing.
6. Whether atoms or nature, let this be laid down first: that I am a part of the Whole, governed by nature; next, that I stand in a certain kinship with the parts of the same kind as myself. For remembering these things, in so far as I am a part, I shall be discontented with nothing that is allotted by the Whole; for nothing that is of benefit to the Whole is harmful to the part. For the Whole has nothing that is not of benefit to itself; all natures have this in common, but the nature of the universe has this further property, that it cannot be compelled by any cause from without to beget anything harmful to itself. So, then, by remembering that I am a part of such a Whole, I shall be content with all that comes to pass; and in so far as I stand in a certain kinship with the parts of the same kind, I shall do nothing against the fellowship, but rather aim at the good of my kind, and direct every impulse of mine toward the common benefit, and turn it away from the contrary. And these things being so accomplished, life must needs flow smoothly — as you might conceive the life of a citizen to flow smoothly, who goes forward through acts of benefit to his fellow citizens, and welcomes whatever the city allots to him.

title: Meditations
text:
7. The parts of the Whole — all that are by nature contained in the universe — must of necessity perish; and let this be understood to signify being altered. But if this is by nature both an evil and a necessity to them, the Whole could not be well conducted, with its parts going on to alteration and being constituted in divers ways for perishing. For did nature herself set about doing harm to her own parts, and making them liable to fall into evil, and of necessity falling into it? Or did such things come to pass without her knowledge? Both are incredible. But if a man should leave nature out of account and explain these things as merely natural, even so it is absurd at once to say that the parts of the Whole are by nature subject to change, and at the same time to wonder at, or be vexed by, something happening as though contrary to nature — especially when the dissolution is into the very things of which each thing is composed. For it is either a scattering of the elements out of which it was compounded, or a turning of the solid into the earthy and of the airy into air, so that even these are taken up into the reason of the Whole, whether that be consumed by fire in cycles or renewed by everlasting exchanges. And do not picture the solid and the airy as that which was there from the first birth; for all this took on its inflow only yesterday or the day before, from the foods and the air drawn in; it is, then, this which it took on that changes, not what your mother bore. And suppose that this binds you closely to that thing of such-and-such a peculiar quality; that, I think, is nothing to the present argument.
8. Having given yourself these names — good, modest, truthful, sensible, of one mind with all, of a mind above all — take heed never to be renamed; and if you lose these names, return to them quickly. And remember that "sensible" was meant to signify for you the discerning attention to each thing and the freedom from carelessness; "of one mind with all," the willing acceptance of what is allotted by the common nature; and "of a mind above all," the lifting of the thinking part above the smooth or rough motion of the flesh, above the little fame, above death, and all such things. If, then, you keep yourself in these names, not craving to be called by them by others, you will be another man and will enter upon another life. For to be still such as you have been until now, and to be torn and defiled in such a life, is the mark of one utterly senseless, in love with life, and like those half-devoured beast-fighters who, covered with wounds and gore, yet beg to be kept till the morrow, to be thrown, such as they are, to the same claws and fangs. Embark, then, upon these few names; and if you can abide in them, abide, as one removed to some Isles of the Blessed. But if you perceive that you are falling away and losing your hold, withdraw with good courage into some corner where you will keep it, or even depart altogether from life — not in anger, but simply, freely, and modestly, having at least done this one thing well in life, that you have so departed. And toward the remembering of these names it will greatly help you to remember the gods, and that they do not wish to be flattered, but that all rational beings should be made like to themselves, and that the fig-tree should do the work of a fig-tree, the dog of a dog, the bee of a bee, and the man of a man.
9. Mime, war, panic, torpor, slavery: day by day these will blot out those holy principles of yours, which you imagine and dismiss without natural reflection. But one must so look at and do everything that at the same time the practical task is accomplished and the contemplative activity is exercised, and the self-confidence that comes from the knowledge of each thing is preserved, unobtrusive but not hidden. For when will you enjoy simplicity? When dignity? When the recognition of each thing — what it is in its essence, what place it holds in the universe, how long it is by nature fitted to subsist, of what it is composed, to whom it can belong, and who can give it and take it away?

title: Meditations
text:
10. The spider is proud when it has caught a fly; one man when he has snared a hare, another a sprat in his net, another little boars, another bears, another Sarmatians. Are these not robbers, if you examine their principles?
11. Acquire a method of contemplating how all things change into one another, and attend to it continually, and exercise yourself in this part; for nothing is so apt to produce greatness of mind. Such a man has stripped off the body, and, reflecting that very soon he must leave all these things behind and depart from among men, has given himself up wholly to justice in what he himself does, and to the Nature of the Whole in all else that befalls. What anyone will say or think of him, or do against him, he does not even take into his mind, being content with these two things: that he himself acts justly in what is now being done, and loves what is now allotted to him. And he has let go all distractions and ambitions, and wishes nothing else than to run a straight course through the law, and, running it, to follow God.
12. What need is there of suspicion, when it is in your power to consider what ought to be done? And if you see it clearly, to go that way kindly and without swerving; but if you do not see it clearly, to hold back and take counsel with the best advisers; and if some other things stand against these, to go forward with deliberation according to the means at hand, holding fast to what appears just? For it is best to hit upon this; since to fail is to fail in just this. Composed and at the same time quick to move, cheerful and at the same time steady, is he who in all things follows reason.
13. Ask yourself, the moment you are roused from sleep: will it make any difference to you if what is just and good is blamed by another? It will not. Have you forgotten that these men who give themselves airs in their praise and blame of others are such as they are upon their bed, such at their table; what they do, what they shun, what they pursue, what they steal, what they snatch — not with hands and feet, but with that most precious part of themselves, by which, when it wills, are produced good faith, modesty, truth, law, a good guardian spirit?
14. To the nature that gives all and takes all back, the man who is instructed and modest says: "Give what you will, take back what you will." And he says this not in defiance, but only in obedience and goodwill toward her.
15. Little is this that is left to you. Live as upon a mountain; for it makes no difference whether one lives there or here, if one lives everywhere as in a city, the universe. Let men see, let them mark, a true man living according to nature. If they cannot bear him, let them kill him; for that is better than to live as they do.
16. No longer talk at all about what manner of man the good man should be, but be such.
17. Continually picture to yourself the whole of time and the whole of substance, and that all particular things are, as to substance, a grain of millet, and as to time, the turning of a gimlet.
18. Fixing your attention on each of the things before you, picture it as even now being dissolved and in change, as it were rotting and scattering, or as each thing is by nature, dying, so to speak.
19. What manner of men they are when they eat, sleep, couple, ease themselves, and the rest; and then what manner of men when they lord it and give themselves airs, or are harsh and rebuke from on high — though a little while ago they were slaves, and to how many, and for what; and a little while hence they will be in such states again.

title: Meditations
text:
20. That is of benefit to each which the Nature of the Whole brings to each; and it is of benefit at the time when she brings it.
21. "The earth loves the rain, and the august heaven loves to give it," and the universe loves to make whatever is to come to be. To the universe, then, I say: I love along with you. And is it not said in this way too, that "this is wont to come to pass"?
22. Either you live here and have grown used to it; or you are going away, and that was your own wish; or you die, and have finished your service. Beyond these there is nothing. Be of good cheer, then.
23. Let it always be clear to you that this place is such a thing as a country field, and how all things here are the same as on the mountain-top, or on the seashore, or wherever you will. For you will find the saying of Plato hold good before your eyes: "fencing himself a fold upon a mountain," he says, "and milking the bleating flocks."
24. What is my ruling faculty to me, and what manner of thing am I now making it, and to what use am I now putting it? Is it empty of mind? Is it loosed and torn away from fellowship? Is it so melted into and mingled with the poor flesh as to be turned about with it?
25. He who flees his master is a runaway; and the master is the law, and so he who breaks the law is a runaway. And likewise he who is grieved, or angry, or afraid, does not wish that something should have come to be, or be coming to be, or be about to be, of the things ordained by him who governs all, who is law, apportioning to each what falls to his lot. He, then, who is afraid, or grieved, or angry, is a runaway.
26. A man lets go the seed into a womb and departs, and thereafter another cause takes it up and works upon it and brings to completion a babe — out of what a thing, what a thing! Again, he lets food down through the throat, and thereafter another cause takes it up and produces perception and impulse, and, in a word, life and strength, and other things — how many and what kind! Contemplate, then, these things that come to pass in such a hidden way, and see the power, as we see the power that bears things down and that bears them up — not with the eyes, yet no less clearly.
27. Reflect continually how all things, such as now come to pass, came to pass before, and reflect that they will come to pass again; and set before your eyes whole dramas and scenes of the same kind, all that you have known from your own experience or from the older histories — as the whole court of Hadrian, the whole court of Antoninus, the whole court of Philip, of Alexander, of Croesus; for all those were of the same kind, only with other actors.
28. Picture to yourself every man who is grieved or discontented at anything whatever as like a pig being sacrificed, kicking and squealing. Like him too is the man who upon his bed bewails his lot alone, in silence. And reflect that only to the rational being is it given to follow willingly the things that come to pass; but to follow simply is laid upon all of necessity.
29. On each of the things you do, stop and ask yourself whether death is dreadful because it robs you of this.
30. When you take offence at someone's fault, turn at once and reflect what like fault you yourself commit — judging money, for instance, to be good, or pleasure, or a little fame, and so forth. For dwelling on this you will quickly forget your anger, when it also occurs to you that he is under compulsion; for what else can he do? Or, if you can, take away that which compels him.

title: Meditations
text:
31. When you see Satyrion, picture to yourself a follower of Socrates, or Eutyches or Hymen; and when you see Euphrates, picture Eutychion or Silvanus; and when you see Alciphron, picture Tropaeophorus; and when you see Severus, picture Crito or Xenophon; and when you look at yourself, picture one of the Caesars, and in each case the like. Then let this thought come home to you: where, then, are those men? Nowhere, or who knows where. For thus you will continually behold human things as smoke and nothing, especially if you remember that what has once changed will be no more through endless time. Why, then, do you strain? Why is it not enough for you to pass through this brief span in seemly fashion? What material and what occasion you are fleeing! For what are all these things but exercises for a reason that has looked closely and in the manner of natural philosophy at the things in life? Abide, then, until you have made even these your own, as a strong stomach makes all things its own, as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever you throw in.
32. Let it be in no one's power to say truly of you that you are not simple, or that you are not good; but let him lie who shall suppose any such thing of you. And all this is in your power; for who is hindering you from being good and simple? Only resolve to live no longer if you are not to be such; for not even reason requires that one be alive who is not such.
33. What is it that, in this matter before you, can be done or said in the soundest way? For whatever that may be, it is in your power to do or say it; and do not make excuses as though you were hindered. You will not cease groaning until you feel this: that to do what is proper to the constitution of man, upon the material laid before you and presenting itself, is to you what luxury is to the lover of pleasure. For you must reckon as an enjoyment everything that it is in your power to do according to your own nature; and it is in your power everywhere. Now to the cylinder it is not granted everywhere to be borne by its own motion, nor to water, nor to fire, nor to the other things governed by nature or by an irrational soul; for the things that bar and stand in the way are many. But mind and reason can pass through everything that opposes them just as their nature and their will require. Setting before your eyes this facility, by which reason will be borne through all things, as fire upward, as a stone downward, as a cylinder down a slope, seek nothing further; for the other obstacles either belong to the body, the corpse, or, apart from opinion and the yielding of reason itself, do not crush us, nor do any evil at all. Otherwise, indeed, the man who suffered would straightway become bad; for in the case of all other contrivances, whatever evil befalls any of them makes the thing itself that suffers worse; but here, if one may say so, a man becomes even better and more praiseworthy by using rightly the things that befall. And in sum, remember that nothing harms the natural citizen which does not harm the city, nor anything the city which does not harm the law; and of these so-called misfortunes none harms the law. What, then, does not harm the law harms neither city nor citizen.
34. To one who is steeped in the true principles, even the briefest and most familiar saying suffices for a reminder against grief and fear, such as: "The leaves the wind scatters to the ground; so is the race of men." Little leaves are your children too; little leaves are these who cry out as though worthy of trust and sound your praises, or, on the contrary, curse you, or in secret blame and mock; and little leaves likewise are those who shall hand on your fame hereafter. For all these "come into being in the season of spring." Then the wind has cast them down; and afterward the wood puts forth others in their place. And short duration is common to all; yet you flee and pursue all things as though they were to be everlasting. In a little while you will close your eyes, and another will be lamenting him who carried you out.

title: Meditations
text:
35. The healthy eye must look at all things visible, and not say, "I want green things"; for that is the mark of the diseased eye. And the healthy hearing and smell must be ready for all that can be heard and smelled; and the healthy stomach disposed alike toward all nourishment, as a mill toward all that it was made to grind. And so the healthy mind must be ready for all that befalls; but that which says, "Let my children be safe," and, "Let all praise whatever I do," is an eye seeking green things, or teeth seeking the tender.
36. There is no one so fortunate that, when he is dying, some will not stand by who welcome the evil that has befallen him. Was he earnest and wise? At the very last there will be someone to say within himself, "We shall breathe again at last, freed from this schoolmaster; he was harsh to none of us, but I felt that he silently condemned us." This, then, is said of the earnest man; but in our own case, how many other reasons there are for which many wish to be rid of us! Reflect on this, then, as you die, and you will depart the more easily, reasoning thus: I am going away from such a life, in which even the partners for whom I strove so much, prayed, and took thought — those very men wish me gone, hoping perhaps for some relief from it. Why, then, should anyone cling to a longer stay here? Yet do not on this account depart less kindly toward them, but keep your own character, friendly, well-disposed, gracious; and again, not as one torn away, but as in a good death the poor soul slips easily out of the body, such should your departure from these men be. For nature bound you to them and blended you with them, but now she dissolves the bond. I am dissolved, as from kinsmen, yet not held back, but without constraint; for this too is one of the things according to nature.
37. Accustom yourself, on everything that anyone does, so far as may be, to ask within yourself: to what does this man refer this? But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.
38. Remember that it is that hidden thing within which pulls the strings: that is the power of speech, that is life, that, if one may say so, is the man. Never picture along with it the surrounding vessel and these organs moulded round it; for they are like an adze, differing only in that they grow upon us. For these parts are of no more use without the cause that moves and checks them than the shuttle is to the weaver, or the pen to the writer, or the whip to the charioteer.
1. The properties of the rational soul: it sees itself, it articulates itself, it makes itself such as it wills, the fruit it bears it gathers itself — whereas the fruits of plants, and what answers to them in animals, others gather; it attains its own end, wherever the close of life may overtake it. For not as in dancing and acting and such things, where the whole performance is left incomplete if anything cuts it short, but at every point, and wherever it may be cut off, the rational soul makes what it set before itself full and lacking nothing, so that it can say, "I have what is mine." Moreover, it ranges over the whole universe and the void around it and its shape, and stretches out into the infinity of time, and embraces and reflects upon the periodic rebirth of the Whole, and considers that those who come after us will see nothing new, and those before us saw nothing more — but that, in a manner, the man of forty, if he has any intelligence at all, has seen all that has been and all that shall be, by reason of their uniformity. And it is proper to the rational soul also to love one's neighbours, and truth, and modesty, and to honour nothing above itself — which is proper to law as well; so that there is, after all, no difference between right reason and the reason of justice.

title: Meditations
text:
2. You will despise the charm of song, and dancing, and the pancratium, if you cut up the tuneful voice into its several notes and ask yourself, of each one, whether you are overcome by it; for you will be ashamed to own it. And in the case of dancing do the like with each movement and posture, and the same with the pancratium. In short, then — except for virtue and what comes of virtue — remember to run to the several parts, and by dividing them to come to despise the thing; and transfer this to the whole of life as well.
3. What manner of soul is that which is ready, if even now it must be released from the body, whether to be quenched, or scattered, or to abide. But let this readiness come from a judgment of its own, not from sheer obstinacy, as with the Christians, but reasoned, and with dignity, and so as to persuade another too, without theatrical display.
4. Have I done something for the common good? Then I am benefited. Let this be ever ready to meet you, and never leave off.
5. What is your art? To be good. And how is this rightly done except by principles — some concerning the Nature of the Whole, others concerning the proper constitution of man?
6. At first tragedies were brought in as reminders of the things that befall, and that these are by nature bound to come to pass, and that you should not be grieved on the greater stage by the very things with which you are charmed on the lesser; for you see that they must be played out in this way, and that even those who cry "Alas, Cithaeron!" bear them. And certain useful things are said by the writers of the dramas, such as, above all, this: "If I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, even this has its reason"; and again, "Against things, indeed, there is no need to feel anger"; and, "Life is reaped like a ripe ear of corn"; and the like. After tragedy the old comedy was brought in, with its instructive frankness, reminding men, not unprofitably, of freedom from conceit by its very plainness of speech; for some such purpose Diogenes too took up these things. After this consider for what purpose the middle comedy was taken up, and then the new, which little by little slipped away into a mere artful imitation. For that some useful things are said even by these is not unknown; but to what end, after all, did the whole aim of such poetry and dramaturgy look?
7. How clearly it comes home to you that there is no other condition of life so fitted for philosophizing as this in which you now happen to be.
8. A branch cut off from the branch next to it cannot but be cut off also from the whole plant. So too a man severed from one man has fallen away from the whole fellowship. Now a branch is cut off by another; but a man cuts himself off from his neighbour by hating him and turning away, and does not know that he has thereby severed himself from the whole commonwealth as well. Yet there is this gift of Zeus, who established the fellowship: it is in our power to grow together again with that to which we are next, and again to become parts that complete the Whole. But if such a severance is repeated often, it makes that which withdraws hard to reunite and hard to restore. And in general the branch which has grown together from the first and shared the common life is not like the one grafted on again after being cut off, whatever the gardeners may say. Grow on the same stem, but not on the same principles.
9. As those who stand in your way, when you go forward according to right reason, cannot turn you aside from sound action, so let them not strike out of you your kindness toward them; but guard yourself equally on both points — not only in steadfast judgment and action, but also in gentleness toward those who try to hinder you or are otherwise vexatious. For to be angry with them is as much a weakness as to forsake the action and give way in dismay; for both alike are deserters from the ranks — the one through fear, the other through being estranged from his natural kinsman and friend.

title: Meditations
text:
10. "No nature is inferior to art"; for the arts imitate natures. And if this is so, the nature which is most perfect of all and most comprehensive could not fall short of the inventiveness of art. Now all the arts make the lower things for the sake of the higher; therefore the common nature does so too. And hence comes the origin of justice, and from justice the other virtues take their being; for the just will not be preserved if we either set our hearts on things indifferent, or are easily deceived, hasty, and changeable.
11. If the things whose pursuit and avoidance trouble you do not come to you, but you in a manner go to them, then at least let your judgment about them keep quiet, and they will remain unmoved, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor fleeing.
12. The soul is a sphere true to its own form, when it neither stretches out toward anything, nor shrinks inward, nor is scattered, nor sinks down, but is lit with the light by which it sees the truth of all things and the truth within itself.
13. Will someone despise me? He shall see to it. But I will see to it that I be found doing or saying nothing worthy of contempt. Will he hate me? He shall see to it. But I am kindly and well-disposed to all, and ready to show even this very man what he has overlooked — not in reproach, nor in a parade of forbearance, but genuinely and kindly, like that famous Phocion, if indeed he was not feigning. For such things must be within, and a man must be seen by the gods to be one not disposed to indignation at anything, nor making a grievance of it. For what evil is it to you, if you yourself are now doing what is proper to your nature, and accepting what is now timely for the Nature of the Whole — a man bent on the coming-to-pass, by whatever means, of the common good?
14. Despising one another, they fawn upon one another; and wishing to surpass one another, they bow down before one another.
15. How rotten and counterfeit is the man who says, "I have resolved to deal frankly with you." What are you doing, man? This need not be announced beforehand; it will appear of itself. It ought to be written on the forehead; the voice should at once ring with it, it should at once flash from the eyes, just as the beloved at once reads everything in the lover's glance. In short, the simple and good man ought to be like one who smells of the goat, so that the bystander, the moment he comes near, whether he will or no, perceives it. But a studied simplicity is a dagger. There is nothing more shameful than the friendship of the wolf; of all things shun this most. The good, the simple, the kindly man has these things in his eyes, and they are not hidden.
16. The power of living the noblest of lives is in the soul, if a man be indifferent to things indifferent. And he will be indifferent, if he contemplates each of them part by part and as a whole, and remembers that none of them produces in us any opinion about itself, nor comes to us; but they stand unmoved, and it is we who beget the judgments about them and, as it were, write them within ourselves — though it is in our power not to write, and in our power, if perchance it has escaped us, at once to blot them out. And remember that such attention will be needed but a little while, and then life will be over. And what hardship is there, after all, in these things being as they are? For if they are according to nature, rejoice in them, and let them be easy for you; but if contrary to nature, seek what is according to your own nature, and hasten to it, even if it bring no fame; for everyone is to be forgiven who seeks his own proper good.

title: Meditations
text:
17. Whence each thing has come, and out of what materials each is composed, and into what it changes, and what it will be when it has changed, and how it will suffer no evil.
18. And first, what is my relation to these men, and that we have come into being for one another's sake; and, on another account, that I have come into being to be set over them, as a ram over a flock or a bull over a herd. And go back to the beginning, from this: if not atoms, then a nature governing the Whole; and if this, the lower for the sake of the higher, and these for one another. Second, what manner of men they are at table, in bed, and the rest; and above all, under what necessities of principles they lie, and with what conceit they do these very things. Third, that if they do these things rightly, we ought not to be vexed; and if not rightly, then plainly against their will and through ignorance. For every soul is robbed against its will of the truth, and likewise of dealing with each man according to his desert. At any rate, men are vexed to be called unjust, ungrateful, grasping, and, in a word, wrongdoers against their neighbours. Fourth, that you yourself do many wrong things, and are such another; and even if you abstain from certain wrongs, still you have a disposition prone to them, even if through cowardice, or care for reputation, or some such baseness, you abstain from the like wrongs. Fifth, that you have not even ascertained that they are doing wrong; for many things are done by way of management, and in general one must learn many things before one can pronounce with sureness about another's act. Sixth, that when you are exceedingly vexed or out of patience, man's life is but a moment, and in a little while we have all been laid out. Seventh, that it is not their acts that trouble us — for these are in their own ruling faculties — but our own opinions. Take away, then, and consent to let go, the judgment that this is something dreadful, and your anger is gone. How, then, will you take it away? By reasoning that it is no disgrace; for unless the disgraceful alone is evil, you too must needs do many wrong things, and become a robber and all manner of man. Eighth, how much heavier are the consequences of the anger and grief we feel at such things than the things themselves at which we are angry and grieved. Ninth, that kindness is invincible, if it be genuine and not a grimace or a pretence. For what will the most insolent man do to you, if you continue kindly toward him, and, should occasion serve, gently admonish and teach him better, at the very moment when he attempts to do you harm? "No, my child; we are made for something else. I shall not be harmed, but you are harming yourself, my child." And show him, deftly and as a general truth, that this is so — that not even bees do such a thing, nor any creatures made for the herd. And you must do this without irony, and without reproach, but with affection and with no rankling in the soul, and not as in a lecture-room, nor that another standing by may admire, but as toward one alone, even if others are standing round. Remember these nine heads, as gifts received from the Muses, and begin at last to be a man, while you live. But you must guard against flattering them no less than against being angry with them; for both alike are against the fellowship and lead to harm. And keep this ready in your fits of anger: that it is not anger that is manly, but that gentleness and mildness, as they are more human, so are they more manly; and that it is the gentle man who has a share of strength, sinew, and courage — not he who is indignant and discontented. For the nearer such a man is to freedom from passion, the nearer is he to power. And as grief is the mark of weakness, so is anger; for both alike are wounded and have given way. And, if you will, take a tenth gift from the Leader of the Muses: that to expect the bad not to do wrong is madness, for it is to wish for the impossible. But to allow that they may be such toward others, while expecting that they do no wrong against you, is senseless and tyrannical.

title: Meditations
text:
19. Four turnings, above all, of the ruling faculty you must watch for continually, and, when you detect them, blot them out, saying in each case: this fancy is not necessary; this is destructive of fellowship; this you are about to say not from yourself — and to speak not from oneself you must reckon among the most monstrous of things. And the fourth is that for which you will reproach yourself: that this is the mark of the diviner part in you being overcome and bowing down before the meaner and mortal part, the body and its rough or smooth motions.
20. Your breath, and all your fiery part, mingled though it is, and by nature upward-tending, yet, in obedience to the ordering of the Whole, is held here upon the compound. And all the earthy and watery part in you, downward-tending though it is, is yet raised up and stands in a posture not its own by nature. So, then, even the elements obey the Whole, when somewhere they are assigned their place by force, and abide there until the signal is given from thence again for their dissolution. Is it not, then, a strange thing that your intelligent part alone should be disobedient and discontented with its place? And yet nothing forcible is laid upon it, but only what is according to its nature; nevertheless it will not endure, but is borne in the contrary direction. For the movement toward wrongdoing and licence, toward anger and grief and fear, is nothing but that of one departing from nature. And whenever the ruling faculty is discontented at anything that befalls, then too it forsakes its own place; for it was framed for holiness and the worship of the gods no less than for justice. For these too are forms of good fellowship — nay, are older than acts of justice.
21. "He who has not always one and the same aim in life cannot be one and the same throughout his life." But the saying does not suffice, unless you add what manner of thing this aim should be. For just as the opinion is not the same about all the things that, in one way or another, seem good to the many, but only about certain things, that is, the common goods, so too one must set up the aim as a common and social one. For he who directs all his own impulses toward this will make all his actions of one kind, and so will always be one and the same.
22. The country mouse and the town mouse, and the terror and scurrying of the one.
23. Socrates used to call the opinions of the many "bogeys," scarecrows for children.
24. The Lacedaemonians, at their spectacles, set seats in the shade for strangers, but themselves sat down wherever they chanced to be.
25. Socrates, on why he would not go to Perdiccas: "Lest," he said, "I perish by the most wretched of ends" — that is, lest, having received a good turn, I be unable to return it.
26. In the writings of the Epicureans there was laid down a precept continually to call to mind one of the men of old who practised virtue.
27. The Pythagoreans bid us look up to the heavens at dawn, that we may be reminded of those bodies which forever, in the same way and after the same fashion, accomplish their own work; and of their order, their purity, their nakedness — for there is no veil over a star.
28. What manner of man was Socrates, girt in the sheepskin, when Xanthippe took the cloak and went out; and what Socrates said to his companions, who were ashamed and drew back when they saw him so attired.
29. In writing and reading you will not lead before you have been led. This is far more true in life.
30. You were born a slave; you have no share in reason.

title: Meditations
text:
31. "And my own dear heart laughed within me."
32. "And they will revile virtue, uttering harsh words."
33. To look for a fig in winter is to be mad; such is he who looks for his child when it is no longer granted.
34. As one kisses his child, Epictetus used to say, one should whisper within, "Perhaps tomorrow you will die." "These are words of ill omen." "Nothing is of ill omen," he said, "that signifies some work of nature; or else it would be of ill omen to say that the ears of corn are reaped."
35. The unripe grape, the ripe, the dried — all are changes, not into nothing, but into what is not yet.
36. "No one robs us of our free choice" — the saying of Epictetus.
37. "We must," he said, "find an art about assent, and in the field of the impulses keep watchful care, that they be made with reservation, that they serve the fellowship, that they be according to desert; and we must hold off altogether from desire, and use aversion toward none of the things not in our power."
38. "It is, then, no common matter," he said, "for which the contest is, but whether we shall be mad or not."
39. Socrates used to say: "What do you wish — to have the souls of rational beings or of irrational?" "Of rational." "Of what rational beings — sound or vicious?" "Sound." "Why, then, do you not seek them?" "Because we have them." "Why, then, do you fight and quarrel?"
1. All those things which you pray to attain by a roundabout course you can have even now, if you do not grudge them to yourself. That is, if you let go all the past, and entrust the future to providence, and direct the present alone toward holiness and justice. Holiness, that you may love what is allotted to you; for nature brought it to you, and you to it. Justice, that you may speak the truth freely and without disguise, and do the things that are according to law and according to desert. And let nothing hinder you — neither the vice of another, nor any opinion, nor a voice, nor even the sensations of the poor flesh that has grown about you; for that which suffers will see to that. If, then, whenever you come near to your departure, leaving all else behind, you honour your ruling faculty alone and the divine within you, and fear not that you must one day cease to live, but rather that you have never yet begun to live according to nature, then you will be a man worthy of the universe that begot you, and you will cease to be a stranger in your own country, and to wonder, as at unexpected things, at what happens day by day, and to hang upon this thing and that.
2. God beholds all the ruling faculties stripped of their material vessels and husks and dross; for with his own intelligence alone he touches only those things that have flowed and been drawn off from himself into them. And if you too accustom yourself to do this, you will rid yourself of much that distracts you; for he who does not look at the flesh that wraps him will surely not, by gazing at clothes and house and fame and such trappings and stage-show, busy himself in vain.
3. Three things there are of which you are composed: a little body, a little breath, and mind. Of these, the first two are yours only in so far as you must take care of them; the third alone is properly your own. If, then, you separate from yourself — that is, from your mind — all that others do or say, and all that you yourself have done or said, and all that troubles you as things to come, and all that belongs without your choice to the poor body that wraps you and the breath bound up with it, and all that the whirl eddying about you whirls along — so that the intelligent power, lifted free of the chain of destiny and kept pure, lives detached upon itself, doing what is just and willing what befalls and speaking the truth; if, I say, you separate from this ruling faculty the things attached to it through the passions, and the things of time beyond or behind it, and make yourself such as Empedocles' "sphere, rounded, rejoicing in its circling rest," and practise to live only that which you live, that is, the present — then you will be able to pass the remainder of your time until death untroubled, kindly, and at peace with your own guardian spirit.

title: Meditations
text:
4. Often I have wondered how it is that, while each man loves himself above all, he yet sets less store by his own opinion of himself than by the opinions of others. At any rate, if a god or a wise teacher stood by and bade a man think and devise nothing within himself which he would not, at the very moment of conceiving it, speak aloud, he could not endure it for a single day. So much more do we stand in awe of what our neighbours will think of us than of ourselves.
5. How is it that the gods, who have ordered all things well and in love of man, have overlooked this one thing only: that some men, even the truly good, who have made, as it were, the most covenants with the divine, and through holy works and rites have become most familiar with the godhead, should yet, once they are dead, never come to be again, but be utterly extinguished? But if indeed this is so, be assured that, had it needed to be otherwise, the gods would have made it so; for had it been just, it would also have been possible, and had it been according to nature, nature would have brought it to pass. From its not being so, then — if indeed it is not so — let it be confirmed for you that it needed not to be so. For you yourself see that, in seeking after this, you are pleading a case of justice with God; and we should not so reason with the gods, were they not most good and most just. And if this is so, they would not have suffered anything in the ordering of the world to be unjustly and unreasonably neglected.
6. Train yourself even in those things which you despair of doing. For the left hand too, idle in other things through want of practice, holds the bridle more strongly than the right; for in this it has been trained.
7. What manner of man one ought to be when overtaken by death, in body and in soul; the shortness of life; the vast gulf of time behind and before; the frailty of all matter.
8. To behold the causal principles stripped of their husks; the references of actions; what pain is; what pleasure; what death; what fame; who it is that makes himself the cause of his own unrest; how no one is hindered by another; that all is opinion.
9. In the use of your principles you should be like the pancratiast, not the gladiator; for the gladiator lays down the sword he uses and takes it up again, but the other always has his hand, and need do nothing but clench it.
10. See things as they are, dividing them into the material, the causal, and the reference.
11. How great a power a man has to do nothing but what God will approve, and to accept all that God apportions to him! Whatever follows from nature.
12. Neither must the gods be blamed — for they do no wrong, willingly or unwillingly — nor men, for they do nothing save unwillingly. Therefore no one is to be blamed.
13. How laughable and what a stranger to the world is he who wonders at anything that comes to pass in life!
14. Either the necessity of destiny and an order not to be transgressed, or a providence that may be appeased, or a confusion of mere chance, without a governor. If, then, it is a necessity not to be transgressed, why do you struggle against it? But if it is a providence that admits of being appeased, make yourself worthy of the help of the divine. But if it is a confusion without a guide, be content that, in such a surge, you yourself have within you a certain governing mind; and though the surge carry you away, let it carry away the poor flesh, the poor breath, and the rest; for it will not carry away the mind.

title: Meditations
text:
15. Or shall the light of the lamp, until it is quenched, shine and not lose its brightness, while the truth and justice and self-control in you are quenched before the end?
16. Concerning him who has given you the impression that he has done wrong: "But how do I know that this is a wrong?" And even if he has done wrong, that he has condemned himself, and so this is like tearing his own face. Reflect, too, that he who would have the bad man do no wrong is like one who would have the fig-tree yield no juice in its figs, and babes not cry, and the horse not neigh, and all the other things that must be. For what is he to do, having such a disposition? If, then, you are keen-witted, cure this.
17. If it is not fitting, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it. For let your impulse be always to see, in everything, what that very thing is which produces the impression in you, and to unfold it, dividing it into the cause, the material, the reference, and the time within which it must come to an end.
19. Perceive at last that you have within you something better and more divine than the things that produce the passions and, in a word, than the things that jerk you like a puppet. What is my mind now? Is it fear? Is it suspicion? Is it desire? Is it any other such thing?
20. First, do nothing at random, nor without reference to an end. Second, refer your action to no other end than the good of the fellowship.
21. That in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, nor will any of these things you now see, nor any of those now living. For all things are by nature fitted to change and turn and perish, that others may come to be in their turn.
22. That all is opinion, and that opinion is in your power. Take away the opinion, then, when you will, and, as for one who has rounded the headland, there is calm, all things steady, and a bay without a wave.
23. Any single activity whatever, ceasing in its due season, suffers no evil in so far as it has ceased; nor has he who did the deed suffered any evil in this very thing, that it has ceased. In like manner, then, the system made up of all activities, which is life, if it cease in its due season, suffers no evil in this very thing, that it has ceased; nor has he who has brought this series to a close in due season been ill disposed. And the season and the limit are given by nature — sometimes by one's own nature, as in old age, but always by the Nature of the Whole, by the changing of whose parts the whole universe remains forever young and in its prime. And all that is of benefit to the Whole is always fair and in season. The ending of life, then, is for each man no evil, since neither is it shameful — being not within our choice and not against the fellowship — but a good, since for the Whole it is timely and of benefit and borne along with it. For so is he borne of God who is borne in the same course as God, and borne by his judgment toward the same things.
24. These three things you must have ready to hand. First, as to what you do, that you do nothing at random, nor otherwise than as Justice herself would have done it; and as to what befalls from without, that it comes either by chance or by providence; and you are neither to blame chance nor to arraign providence. Second, what each thing is from the seed to the ensouling, and from the ensouling to the giving back of the soul, and out of what it is compounded and into what it is dissolved. Third, that if you were suddenly lifted on high and looked down upon human affairs and their manifold variety, you would despise them, seeing at the same time how great a throng of beings of the air and the upper air dwell round about; and that, however often you were lifted up, you would see the same things, all of one kind, all short-lived. And in these things is our conceit!

title: Meditations
text:
25. Cast out the opinion, and you are saved. Who, then, is hindering you from casting it out?
26. When you are out of patience at anything, you have forgotten that all things come to pass according to the Nature of the Whole; and that the wrong done is another's; and besides this, that all that comes to pass came to pass thus always, and will come to pass, and now comes to pass everywhere; and how great is the kinship of a man with the whole race of men — for it is a fellowship not of a little blood or seed, but of mind. And you have forgotten too that each man's mind is God and has flowed from thence; and that nothing is the private property of any man, but that his child, his body, his very soul have come from thence; and that all is opinion; and that each man lives only the present, and it is this that he loses.
27. Continually call to mind those who have been exceedingly vexed at something, those who reached the height of great fame, or calamities, or enmities, or fortunes of whatever kind; then stop and ask: where is all that now? Smoke and ash and a tale, or not even a tale. And let every such thing come home to you: Fabius Catullinus in his country house, Lusius Lupus in his gardens, Stertinius at Baiae, Tiberius at Capri, and Velius Rufus, and, in a word, every difference made about anything with conceit; and how cheap is everything men strain after, and how much more philosophic it is, upon the material given, to show oneself just, temperate, following the gods, in all simplicity. For the conceit that is conceited about its very freedom from conceit is the most grievous of all.
28. To those who ask, "Where, then, have you seen the gods, or whence have you grasped that they exist, that you so revere them?" — first, they are visible even to the eyes; and again, neither have I seen my own soul, and yet I honour it. So too with the gods: from the experience of their power, in every instance, I grasp that they exist, and I stand in awe of them.
29. The safety of life is to see each thing wholly, what it is in itself — what is its material, what its cause; with the whole soul to do what is just and to speak the truth. What then is left but to enjoy life, joining good to good so as to leave not even the smallest interval between?
30. There is one light of the sun, though it be parted by walls, by mountains, by countless other things. There is one common substance, though it be parted into countless bodies of particular qualities. There is one soul, though it be parted among countless natures and individual bounds. There is one intelligent soul, though it seem to be divided. Now the other parts of the things named — such as breaths and material things — are without sensation and without kinship to one another; yet even these the unifying principle holds together, and their tendency toward the same place. But the mind, in a peculiar way, stretches toward what is of its own kind and joins with it, and the affection for fellowship is not cut off.
31. What do you seek? To go on breathing? But to perceive? To have impulse? To grow? To leave off growing again? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth your longing? But if each is contemptible, go on to the last thing: to follow reason and God. Yet it fights against this to honour these things, to be grieved if by death a man shall be deprived of them.
32. How small a part of the boundless and gaping gulf of time has been apportioned to each man! For very swiftly it vanishes into the everlasting. And how small a part of the whole substance, how small a part of the whole soul! And on how small a clod of the whole earth do you creep! Reflecting on all these things, picture nothing as great except this: to do as your own nature leads you, and to bear what the common nature brings.

title: Meditations
text:
33. How does the ruling faculty use itself? For in this lies the whole. All else, whether within your choice or without it, is dead and smoke.
34. Most rousing toward the contempt of death is that even those who judge pleasure a good and pain an evil have nonetheless despised it.
35. To him for whom only the timely is good; for whom it is all one to render more right actions according to reason or fewer; for whom it makes no difference whether he has gazed upon the universe a longer time or a shorter — to him not even death is a thing to fear.
36. Man, you have been a citizen in this great city; what does it matter to you whether for five years or for three? For what is according to the laws is equal for each. What is dreadful, then, if it is no tyrant nor unjust judge that sends you out of the city, but the nature that brought you in — just as a praetor who engaged a player dismisses him from the stage? "But I have not played the five acts, only three." You say well; but in life the three acts are the whole drama. For he determines the completion who was once the cause of your composition and now of your dissolution; but you are the cause of neither. Depart, then, content; for he who releases you is content also.
